# Competitive Map — BURL

## 1. Dominant Segment

Burlington is a single-segment U.S. off-price retailer: the Burlington store operation produced 100% of FY2025 reported revenue and profit. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Note 1 — Segment Information; data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q-Aug-27-2026.txt (Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q), Note 1 — Segment Reporting]

## 2. Named Competitors

### Competitor A — Ross Stores, Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** NasdaqGS: ROST.
- **Where they compete:** U.S. off-price apparel and home fashion through Ross Dress for Less and dd’s DISCOUNTS. Ross had 1,904 Ross stores and 363 dd’s stores at January 31, 2026; its merchandise and value proposition overlap Burlington’s apparel, footwear, accessories and home categories. [Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 1 — Business]
- **Scale:** $24.512bn LTM revenue in the latest Capital IQ peer filing data (filed September 1, 2026); FY2025 reported sales were $22.751bn. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Financial Data, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — Results of Operations]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Latest LTM EBIT margin was 12.7%. FY2025 operating margin was 11.9%. Calculated FY2025 return on equity (ROE, net earnings divided by average beginning-and-ending stockholders’ equity) was 36.7%: $2.145bn / (($6.187bn + $5.509bn) / 2). This is an equity return, not ROIC. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — Results of Operations; Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income and Balance Sheets]
- **Source named in:** Capital IQ’s BURL comparable-company export includes Ross; Burlington’s own filing names off-price retailers as a competing class but does not name individual companies. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Business Description, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Item 1 — Competition]
- **One-line read:** *Inference, not from filings:* Ross is the closest national, U.S.-only off-price peer in this named set. Its $24.512bn latest LTM revenue is about twice Burlington’s $12.209bn, and it also operates the lower-price dd’s format. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Financial Data and Business Description, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 1 — Business]

### Competitor B — The TJX Companies, Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** NYSE: TJX.
- **Where they compete:** Its U.S. Marmaxx segment operates T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and Sierra. It sold $36.585bn of apparel- and home-led merchandise in FY2026 through 2,748 U.S. locations, making it the direct TJX business to compare with Burlington rather than the full international group. [TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments]
- **Scale:** $62.363bn group LTM revenue in the latest Capital IQ peer filing data; the directly relevant U.S. Marmaxx segment was $36.585bn in FY2026. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Financial Data, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Latest group LTM EBIT margin was 12.2%. Marmaxx’s FY2026 segment-profit margin was 15.1%; it is a pre-tax segment measure before corporate expense and net interest, so it is not the same basis as group EBIT. Calculated FY2026 group ROE was 59.1%: $5.494bn net income / (($10.190bn + $8.393bn) / 2 average shareholders’ equity). This is an equity return, not ROIC. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments; Consolidated Statements of Income and Balance Sheets]
- **Source named in:** Capital IQ’s BURL comparable-company export includes TJX; Burlington’s own filing names off-price retailers as a competing class but does not name individual companies. [data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Business Description, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Item 1 — Competition]
- **One-line read:** T.J. Maxx and Marshalls give TJX a much larger U.S. off-price footprint, while Burlington remains a store-only model and TJX says Marmaxx e-commerce, together with Sierra.com, represented about 2% of Marmaxx sales in FY2026. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Item 1A — Competition; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments]

## 3. Competitive Position

**Position: Gaining store footprint (inference); revenue-market share is not disclosed.** Burlington added 149 net stores in the year to August 1, 2026, taking the chain to 1,287; that is 13.1% growth from the implied 1,138 a year earlier. As a directional reach proxy, this was faster than Ross’s 81 net additions (2,186 to 2,267) and Marmaxx’s 68 (2,680 to 2,748), though the peer reporting windows do not match exactly. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q-Aug-27-2026.txt (Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q), MD&A — Liquidity and Capital Resources / Store Openings; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — Store Openings; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments]

The mature-store signal does not establish a sales-share gain: Burlington’s comparable sales rose 4% in the six months to August 1, 2026, broadly matching TJX Marmaxx’s 4% in FY2026 and below Ross’s 5% in FY2025. Those are different reporting windows, so this is neither a matched comparison nor a market-share series. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q-Aug-27-2026.txt (Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q), MD&A — Six Month Period Ended August 1, 2026; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — Results of Operations]

## 4. Competitive Shape

**Fragmented.** Burlington describes U.S. retail apparel and home-furnishings markets as “highly fragmented and competitive” and identifies competition not only from off-price chains but also department, specialty, online, discount, wholesale-club and outlet retailers. Ross independently uses the same fragmented-market description for apparel and home fashion. The admitted evidence contains no like-for-like market-share, top-four-share or HHI series, so the two named large operators do not justify an oligopoly claim. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Item 1 — Competition; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 1 — Business]

## 5. Caveat

Burlington’s Competition discussion names competitor categories rather than corporate names and does not provide an off-price market-share series. Ross and TJX are credible named rivals because the Capital IQ BURL comparable export identifies them and their own audited filings confirm the directly overlapping U.S. off-price businesses, but BURL revenue share is not proven from available data. A same-boundary U.S. off-price apparel-and-home sales panel, with retailer shares over time, would resolve whether the faster Burlington store rollout is translating into sales-share gains. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K-Mar-19-2026.txt (FY2025 Form 10-K), Item 1 — Competition; data/BURL/Company-Comparable-Analysis-Burlington-Stores-Inc.xls, Business Description, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 1 — Business; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K (SEC), Item 7 — U.S. Segments]

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — BURL

## 1. Named Competitors

- **Ross Stores, Inc. (NasdaqGS: ROST):** U.S. off-price apparel and home-fashion retailer operating Ross Dress for Less and dd’s DISCOUNTS; 2,267 stores at January 31, 2026. [Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2; Ross FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Business]
- **The TJX Companies, Inc. (NYSE: TJX):** its directly relevant U.S. Marmaxx segment operates T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and Sierra, with 2,748 locations and $36.585bn FY2026 sales. [Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2; TJX FY2026 Form 10-K, Item 7 — U.S. Segments]

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | N | Burlington is nationally recognized and offers branded goods at up to 60% below other retailers’ prices, but management says awareness is below that of other retailers and many shoppers still think of the former “Coat Factory.” The customer proposition is value and third-party brands, not a proven BURL brand premium that blocks Ross or TJX. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Business Overview; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A] | 30 |
| Cost advantage | N | The chain buys much merchandise in-season, shifts supplier/category purchases and aims for better supplier terms. Those are useful operating levers, but they are not a proven cost advantage against the named rivals: BURL’s LTM EBIT margin is 7.8% versus Ross’s 12.7% and TJX’s 12.2%. *Inference, not from filings:* a shared off-price model and lower BURL EBIT do not evidence a defendable cost lead. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model; Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2] | 35 |
| Distribution | Y | Six distribution centres shipped more than 99% of FY2025 merchandise units, supported by pool-point facilities; the new Savannah centre began outbound flow in Q2 FY2026. This is a real national operating asset, though larger rivals also run nationwide networks. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Distribution and Warehousing; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A] | 60 |
| Scale | Y | BURL reached 1,287 stores at August 1, 2026, up from 927 at FY2022 end, but Ross had 2,267 and Marmaxx 2,748 locations. The expanding footprint gives purchasing and distribution scale, yet it remains smaller than both named competitors. [BURL FY2024 Annual Report, Item 1 — Store Expansion; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks; Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §§2–3] | 50 |
| Technology / IP | N | Predictive tools, routing and allocation systems helped Q2 supply-chain efficiency, but no proprietary technology, patent, or exclusive data asset that prevents a named competitor from competing is disclosed. *Inference, not from filings.* [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Competition] | 20 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | The disclosed model is conventional U.S. retail. No exclusive licence, regulated concession, or permit that limits Ross or TJX is identified. Not proven from available data. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Business Overview / Competition] | 0 |
| Network effects | N | The “treasure hunt” assortment is intended to encourage repeat visits, but purchases occur at the point of sale and the filings disclose no customer, merchant, or data network whose value rises with every additional user. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Business Overview / Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model] | 5 |
| Switching costs | N | Customers can buy branded apparel and home goods from a wide group of retailers; the Q2 comparable-sales gain was driven primarily by basket size while transactions were relatively flat. There is no contract, subscription or membership tie. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Competition; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A] | 10 |
| Natural resource access | N | BURL owns no manufacturing facilities and sources finished merchandise from vendors, many of which produce overseas. No scarce-resource right is disclosed. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A — Merchandise Sourcing and Import Risks] | 0 |
| Location advantage | N | Its existing 1,287-store footprint is captured under distribution and scale. The filing says growth depends on finding desirable sites and acceptable lease terms, not on exclusive locations. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Store Expansion and Real Estate Strategy; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] | 30 |

## 3. Competitive Economics

BURL reports under US GAAP and all figures below are in USD. “Gross margin” should not be compared mechanically across retailers because BURL puts certain buying, distribution, store-related and depreciation costs outside cost of sales. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7 — Gross Margin]

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Burlington Stores | 44.1% | 7.8% | 7.8% ROIC LTM; 7.0% mean across the five annual readings from Jan. 29, 2022 to Jan. 31, 2026 | LTM to Aug. 1, 2026; annual readings Jan. 2022–Jan. 2026 | CIQ Financials → Income Statement + Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export |
| Ross Stores — ROST | Not disclosed in competitive-map profile | 12.7% | Not disclosed as ROIC; FY2025 calculated ROE was 36.7%, which is not comparable to ROIC | Latest LTM margin; FY2025 ROE | Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2 (retaining its cited CIQ Operating Statistics and Ross FY2025 Form 10-K sources) |
| The TJX Companies — TJX | Not disclosed in competitive-map profile | 12.2% | Not disclosed as ROIC; FY2026 group ROE was 59.1%, which is not comparable to ROIC | Latest group LTM margin; FY2026 ROE | Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2 (retaining its cited CIQ Operating Statistics and TJX FY2026 Form 10-K sources) |

**The economic moat test: Not assessable.** Through-cycle return on capital is **7.0% ROIC** (simple mean of CIQ’s 9.5%, 4.7%, 6.2%, 7.2% and 7.4% annual reads from Jan. 29, 2022 to Jan. 31, 2026; latest LTM is 7.8%), but a matching group WACC is not determinable from the available evidence. The 10-K’s 6.2% weighted-average lease discount rate is a collateralized lease incremental-borrowing-rate input, not group WACC; CIQ supplies a 1.42 five-year beta but no source-bound equity-risk premium or market-return input. Constructing CAPM from that missing input would be an unsourced inference, so no cost of capital is invented. [CIQ Financials → Income Statement + Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export; FY2025 Form 10-K, Leases note; CIQ Comparable Analysis → Operating Statistics, as of 2026-09-28 — vendor export]

The BURL LTM ROIC is a reconciled vendor read: the deterministic `ciq_facts.json` reports 7.8% with `status: present`, and the underlying CIQ ratios sheet shows 7.8259%; there is no material gap. [CIQ Financials → Income Statement + Ratios (multi-year columns), retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export]

**ROIC cross-check and tax basis.** Management does not disclose a group ROIC headline. For FY2025, reported operating income of $864.3m × (1 − 25.3% normalized tax rate) gives $645.7m NOPAT (after-tax operating profit). The 25.3% rate is the simple average of FY2024’s 25.4% and FY2025’s 25.2%; Q2 FY2026’s lower interim rate is excluded because the filing says it benefited from purchased federal energy tax credits. On a gross-capital basis, average FY2024–FY2025 debt-equivalent operating leases plus equity were $8,391.6m and $9,497.4m, respectively: ($8,391.6m + $9,497.4m) / 2 = $8,944.5m; $645.7m / $8,944.5m = **7.2%**. That is 20bp below CIQ’s 7.4% FY2025 ROIC, so the conservative calculated result is used as the cross-check. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7 — Results of Operations / Income Taxes; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 7 — Income Taxes; CIQ Financials → Balance Sheet and Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export]

## 4. Where The Company Sits

**Relative to peers:** Insufficient data to compare against named peers on both margin and capital efficiency. On the only directly comparable profitability line supplied by competitive-map, BURL’s 7.8% LTM EBIT margin is below Ross’s 12.7% and TJX’s 12.2%; peer ROIC is not disclosed and gross-margin definitions are not safely comparable. [Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §2; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7 — Gross Margin]

**Absolute (the economic moat test):** Not assessable — BURL’s through-cycle ROIC is 7.0% (latest LTM 7.8%), but cost of capital is not determinable from available data without inventing a WACC. [CIQ Financials → Income Statement + Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export; FY2025 Form 10-K, Leases note]

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat — structural, not yet proven economic.** The strongest evidence is the 60/100 distribution asset, reinforced by an expanding but still sub-scale store base and flexible in-season sourcing. It has not translated into peer-leading EBIT economics, and no valid cost-of-capital comparison is available to prove a sustained economic spread; over the next five years, the durability test is whether gross-capital ROIC and EBIT margin rise through the consumer and weather cycle while store growth avoids dilution and competitive response. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Distribution and Warehousing / Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model; Competitive Map — BURL, 2026-09-29, §§2–3]

**Moat trajectory: not assessable (mixed — direction not established).**

| Metric (same 3–5 year window) | Start | Latest | Direction | Supports / contradicts the stated trajectory |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin | 41.6% (Jan. 29, 2022) | 44.1% (LTM) | Up 250bp | Supports a better merchandise/freight outcome, but BURL’s gross-margin classification limits peer comparison. |
| EBITDA margin | 11.0% (Jan. 29, 2022) | 11.1% (LTM) | Roughly flat, +20bp | Neutral. |
| EBIT or operating margin | 8.5% (Jan. 29, 2022) | 7.8% (LTM) | Down 70bp | Contradicts widening. |
| Return on capital (ROIC / ROCE) vs cost of capital | 9.5% ROIC (Jan. 29, 2022) | 7.8% ROIC (LTM); cost of capital not determinable | Down 170bp; spread not assessable | Contradicts widening; it is the decisive unresolved row. |
| Market share (or the closest disclosed volume/position proxy) | 927 stores (FY2022) | 1,287 stores (Q2 FY2026) | Up 38.8% | Supports greater physical reach, not a proven revenue-share gain. |
| Cash conversion (CFO ÷ EBITDA) | 81.6% (FY2022: $833.2m / $1,020.6m) | 104.0% (LTM: $1,415.5m / $1,360.7m) | Up 22.4pp | Supports improved cash conversion, though it does not establish price power. |
| Pricing / realised price or mix | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not assessable | Neither. Q2 had a higher basket and flat transactions, but no realised-price or mix series is disclosed. |

The panel is split rather than confirming either widening or erosion. Gross margin rose from 41.6% to 44.1%, cash conversion rose from 81.6% to 104.0%, and store count rose from 927 to 1,287; these support the operating platform. In contrast, EBIT margin fell from 8.5% to 7.8% and ROIC fell from 9.5% to 7.8%, while market share and realised-price data are not disclosed. The improved gross margin does not overturn those two capital-efficiency rows because BURL itself says its gross-margin classification is not comparable across retailers, and Q2 FY2026 reported gross margin also included $55.5m of tariff refunds that management intends to reinvest; therefore this is not confirmed erosion, but neither is it a widening moat. [CIQ Financials → Income Statement, Cash Flow and Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export; BURL FY2024 Annual Report, Item 1 — Store Expansion; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin / Tariff Refunds; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]

The single next data point most likely to flip this read is **FY2026 gross-capital ROIC**, calculated from reported GAAP operating income, normalized tax and year-end capital in the FY2026 Form 10-K: a rise above FY2025’s 7.4% CIQ read on the same basis would support improvement; a decline would reinforce erosion. *Inference, not management guidance:* it should arrive with the annual filing in roughly March 2027 based on the prior filing cadence; the exact date is not announced. [CIQ Financials → Ratios, retrieved 2026-09-29 — vendor export; FY2025 Form 10-K, filed 2026-03-19]

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — BURL

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices | Mid | Higher input costs can raise merchandise costs and the cost of basic necessities for customers. Burlington can buy more in-season and shift purchases between suppliers and categories, but it does not disclose a commodity sensitivity or a measured offset. | [FY25 10-K, Item 7 MD&A — Inflation]; [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.6] |
| Interest rates | Mid | Rates affect customer credit and household costs. They also affect $1,730.6m of floating-rate debt; swaps reduce, but do not remove, the direct exposure. | [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.6]; [FY25 10-K, Item 7A, pp.39–40] |
| FX | Mid | BURL has one U.S. revenue segment. However, many vendors produce overseas and movements in a vendor's local currency against the U.S. dollar can raise BURL's cost of goods. No FX sensitivity is disclosed. | [FY25 10-K, Note 12 — Segment Information, p.52]; [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.11] |
| Freight / logistics rates | Mid | Inbound and distribution-center freight sit in cost of sales. Port disruption, carrier interruption, reduced freight capacity and alternative routing can increase cost or create inventory shortages; BURL's merchandise reaches stores through its distribution network. | [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, pp.9, 11]; [Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin] |
| Government policy | High | Trade and tariff decisions affect imported merchandise costs and customer prices. The company received a $55.5m tariff refund in Q2 FY26, showing that policy has recently affected reported cost of sales; the current tariff terms as of the run date are not established by the frozen evidence. | [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, pp.6, 11; Note 15 — Subsequent Events]; [Q2 FY26 10-Q, p.20] |
| Regulation | Mid | Minimum-wage, benefits, temporary-labor, employment and ESG requirements can raise operating and compliance costs. The filing does not quantify a regulatory-cost sensitivity. | [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, pp.8, 10] |
| Weather | High | Sales and store traffic depend in part on seasonal conditions: cold Fall weather helps cold-weather apparel and warm early Spring weather helps warm-weather goods. Unseasonable weather can leave inventory mismatched, with a larger effect in the higher-sales second half. Management calls late-September onward weather an important driver of Q3 comparable sales. | [FY25 10-K, Business — Seasonality, p.5]; [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, pp.7–8]; [Q2 FY26 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks and Q&A] |
| Geopolitics | Mid | War, political instability, strikes and health events can disrupt overseas production, ports and transport and can also weaken consumer confidence. The company provides no direct earnings sensitivity. | [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, pp.6, 9, 11] |
| Consumer cycle | High | BURL identifies the low-income shopper as its core customer; inflation, employment, benefits, tax refunds, credit and household costs can change discretionary spend, store traffic and comparable sales. A weaker economy can also make higher-income shoppers more value-conscious, so this is not a one-way relationship. | [Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A — Uncertainties and Challenges, p.22]; [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.6] |

BURL has no disclosed industrial-cycle exposure that merits a separate row. Its one reportable segment derives all revenue in the United States. [FY25 10-K, Note 12 — Segment Information, p.52]

## 1A. Named Policy & Subsidy Register — current status as of 2026-09-29

| Programme (local name + English) | Status as of 2026-09-29 | Terms in the reference period | Terms NOW (or successor programme) | Change, quantified | Stated end date? | Source + date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States IEEPA tariff-refund process / Section 122 global tariff | Status not established from available sources | The FY25 10-K says the Supreme Court limited IEEPA tariff authority on 2026-02-20; U.S. Customs launched an IEEPA-refund system in April. It also says the President announced a Section 122 global tariff effective 2026-02-24 for 150 days, subject to unspecified exemptions. | No dated issuing-authority release establishing the rate, exemptions, extension, or successor through 2026-09-29 is in the frozen pool. | BURL received $55.5m of IEEPA tariff refunds in Q2 FY26, recorded as a reduction of cost of sales. The available sources do not quantify a current tariff-rate change. | A 150-day reference term is disclosed for the Section 122 tariff; current status after that reference term is not established from available sources. | [FY25 10-K, Note 15 — Subsequent Events, filed 2026-03-19]; [Q2 FY26 10-Q, p.20, filed 2026-08-27] |

No other dependency in the table relies on a named subsidy, tax incentive, mandate, tariff, price cap, or replacement programme.

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Disclosed sensitivity | Basis and limitation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest rates | A 100-basis-point increase or decrease would increase or decrease annual cash interest expense by $6.3m. | Based on $1,730.6m of floating-rate debt at 2026-01-31, after interest-rate swaps; assumes borrowing level, financial-instrument mix and other variables stay constant. It is not a consumer-demand sensitivity. | [FY25 10-K, Item 7A, p.40] |

No commodity, FX, freight, tariff, weather, or consumer-spending sensitivity was disclosed in the available filings.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.** BURL's outcomes are materially exposed to lower-income discretionary spending, seasonal weather and overseas production and trade policy. Management has real levers: it buys much merchandise close to need, can shift purchases between suppliers and categories, uses interest-rate swaps, and says it has reduced weather exposure through mix and localization. Those levers reduce exposure but do not make it company-controlled. The $55.5m Q2 FY26 tariff refund is not an ongoing earnings benefit in management's stated full-year plan: it intends to reinvest the amount in customer value across the second half. [FY25 10-K, Business — Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model, p.3]; [Q2 FY26 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**55 / 100 — inverted: higher = worse.**

This is a material-exposure, mixed-mitigation score. Consumer spending and weather are the main operating variables; tariffs and overseas supply add cost and availability risk. The score is below the mostly-externally-driven range because the filing documents flexible procurement and category/supplier shifts, while the company has an interest-rate hedge. No filing quantifies the protection from those operating levers against tariffs, weather or consumer weakness. [FY25 10-K, Item 7 MD&A — Inflation; Item 1A, pp.9–11; Item 7A, pp.39–40]

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

**Consumer cycle:** a sustained 20% adverse hit to the discretionary-spending capacity of BURL's low-income core customer would likely cause the most damage through traffic and comparable sales; the company discloses no numerical sensitivity, and value trade-down is a partial counterforce rather than a proven offset. [Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A — Uncertainties and Challenges, p.22]

## 2. Classification

**Standard professional management** — the evidence shows formal governance controls, stable senior leadership, repurchases that exceed equity issuance on the reported share-count measures, no disclosed related-person transactions, and no serial-acquirer pattern. The counterweight is an unusually large organic capex program, a longer cash-conversion cycle, and substantial lease commitments; these make the allocation outcome dependent on store and supply-chain returns rather than on a governance failure already visible in the filings. [FY2026 Proxy, Corporate Governance; Certain Relationships and Related Person Transactions, p.74; FY2025 10-K, Item 7 — Capital Expenditures, p.33]

## 3. Most Material Signal

The most material signal is capex intensity versus the cash the business generates. FY2025 operating cash flow was $1,231.4m against reported capex of $1,104.1m (including accrued capex), leaving $127.3m on that reported basis; in H1 FY2026, $334.6m of operating cash flow versus $426.7m reported capex (also including accruals) was a $92.1m shortfall. The half-year comparison is seasonal and therefore not a forecast, but a persistent shortfall after a full fiscal year, or no improvement in cash conversion as new stores and distribution centres mature, would move the classification to **Capital allocation concerns**. [FY2025 10-K, Item 7 — Cash Flows and Capital Expenditures, p.33; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Item 2 — Cash Flow and Capital Expenditures, p.30]

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**66 /100 (higher = better).** This is the weighted inverse of the signal severities, placing extra weight on capex, debt including leases, off-balance-sheet commitments, and working capital. No serial-acquirer cap applies: the acquisition-pattern severity is 8/100, not 70/100 or higher. The score is supported by clean disclosed related-person and audit reads, stable leadership, and a declining reported diluted share count, but held in the standard-management band by the $1.104bn FY2025 organic investment program, cash conversion that lengthened through FY2025, and the $3.993bn operating-lease liability. [FY2025 10-K, Item 7 — Capital Expenditures, p.33; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheets; CIQ Financials→Ratios, FY2022–FY2025 annual columns — vendor export]

# Red Flags Sweep — BURL

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

| Upstream Agent | Flag Already Surfaced |
|---|---|
| disqualifier-scan | No hard disqualifier: no qualified audit opinion, material restatement, reported related-person transaction, or three-year negative-operating-cash-flow pattern. |
| segment-map | A single U.S. off-price retail segment carries all reported revenue and profit; high expansion capex and inventory-flow execution risk are already identified. |
| customer-geography | All reported revenue is U.S.-based, with demand exposed to a low-income core customer; customer concentration cannot be tested from the available filings. |
| business-quality | Uncontracted retail demand, intense competition, low recurring revenue, high capital intensity, seasonal earnings, and temporary tariff-refund help to Q2 margin. |
| external-dependency | Consumer spending, weather, tariffs, overseas sourcing, freight, FX and labour/regulation exposure; no measured operating sensitivity beyond interest rates. |
| capital-allocation-governance | Heavy organic capex, a longer cash-conversion cycle, strict net debt of $1,215.9m at 2026-08-01, operating-lease liabilities and purchase commitments; no serial-acquirer, related-party, auditor-change, or leadership-turnover flag. |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Distribution-network concentration | Six distribution centres shipped more than 99% of FY2025 merchandise units. Three were in New Jersey and three in Southern California, so disruption at one or more primary sites can delay store inventory, lose sales and raise cost. The disclosed Georgia facility was expected to be fully operational during FY2026 and Arizona capacity during FY2028, but the available interim filing does not quantify how much the FY2025 concentration has fallen. | FY2025 filing identifies the six centres, their locations and their >99% unit share; it also says loss of significant capacity at a primary centre could significantly disrupt the business. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Distribution and Warehousing, p.2; Item 1A — Distribution Network Risk] | 55 |
| Rising inventory-shrink exposure, with an unquantified margin effect | Burlington says shrinkage and loss-prevention costs increased in recent years. Inventory and gross margin depend on estimates for markdowns and shortage; a 1% change in retail markdown dollars would have increased FY2025 markdown cost by about $2.8m. The filing does not disclose a shrinkage amount or sensitivity, so the present financial effect is not assessable. This is a disclosed estimation risk, not evidence of aggressive accounting. | [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A — Inventory Shrinkage and Safety Risks; Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates — Inventory] | 35 |
| Ongoing wage-and-hour, California PAGA and other legal claims | The company is defending class or collective labour actions, California Private Attorneys’ General Act claims, and commercial, product, employee, customer, privacy and other claims. Outcomes and amounts are not quantified. Management says it does not expect a material adverse effect, so this is a lower-severity contingent-liability risk rather than a proven material loss. | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 11 — Commitments and Contingencies; Item 1 — Legal Proceedings] | 25 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

Distribution-network concentration is the main additional concern. In FY2025, six facilities handled more than 99% of merchandise units, with three located in New Jersey and three in Southern California; Burlington itself says a loss of significant capacity at a primary centre could significantly disrupt inventory delivery. The planned Georgia and Arizona facilities are mitigating actions, but the available filings do not provide the current unit split after those additions. This is an operational point-of-failure risk, separate from the upstream tariff, freight and weather exposures. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Distribution and Warehousing, p.2; Item 1A — Distribution Network Risk]

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

The distribution risk is most consequential in the already-identified higher-sales second half, when Burlington must carry more inventory before the holiday selling period. A disruption then could combine with the upstream seasonality, inventory-management and new-capacity execution risks; this is a connected operating-risk pattern, not a second capex or lease-liability flag. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Seasonality; Item 1 — Distribution and Warehousing, p.2; Item 1A — Distribution Network Risk]

# Earnings Module — BURL (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Burlington’s earnings picture is mixed: Q2 sales and underlying operating margin improved, but annual sales growth had slowed and the quarter was helped by a finite tariff refund. New and non-comparable stores drove $254.8 million, or about 86%, of Q2’s sales increase, while transactions at mature stores were relatively flat. The next-quarter revenue bar sits inside management’s range and looks fair, while the EPS comparison is not definition-matched. The biggest risk is that the $22.2 million Q3 value investment fails to revive traffic and instead raises markdown pressure. The verdict is a mixed earnings setup. [FY2025 10-K, p.43; Q2 FY2026 10-Q, pp.3,20 and MD&A—Net Sales; Q2 FY2026 call, prepared remarks and Q&A; CIQ Estimates, FQ3 FY2027, latest change 2026-09-22]

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict:** Mixed earnings setup
- Earnings clarity /100: **74**
- Earnings quality /100: **73**
- Consensus setup /100 *(higher = more beatable)*: **50**
- Earnings volatility /100 *(higher = worse; inverted)*: **58**
- Data quality /100: **90**
- Overall usefulness /100: **78**
- Next-quarter setup: **Balanced**
- Biggest earnings driver: New and non-comparable stores supplied $254.8 million, about 86%, of Q2’s $296.8 million sales increase. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales]
- Biggest earnings risk: Weak Fall traffic or weather could make the planned $22.2 million Q3 value investment reduce margin without enough sales response, while higher inventory raises markdown exposure. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks and Q&A; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Inventory]
- **Red-flag severity verdict: Material concerns.**

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Q2’s 11.0% sales growth was not broad demand acceleration: 9.4 percentage points came from new and non-comparable stores, while the comparable-store contribution was 1.6 points and transactions were relatively flat. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A]
- **Strongest bull point:** Excluding the tariff refund and bankruptcy-acquired-lease costs, adjusted EBIT margin—adjusted operating profit as a share of sales—improved 100 basis points, and FY2025 cash from operations equalled 99.2% of CIQ-standard EBITDA. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Income Statement]
- **Single killer risk:** The H2 price investment fails to lift transactions during a warm or weak Fall, causing sales, markdowns and selling-cost leverage to worsen together. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks and Q&A; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Inventory]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Q2 underlying merchandise margin added 70 basis points, cash conversion remains sound, and trailing free cash flow (FCF, cash from operations less total capital spending) turned positive; those facts rule out a clean deterioration call even though the latest reported quarter is not a normal run rate. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20]

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| earnings-data-triage | **Sufficient.** No formal partial-data cap is triggered. | Current 10-K, Q2 10-Q, cash flow, verbatim transcript, consensus and revisions are available; all frozen-pool sources extracted successfully. [Earnings Data Triage, Sections 1–6] |
| historical-financials | Annual growth has slowed, but the latest quarter and trailing cash flow improved. | Q2 sales rose 11.0% and CIQ-standard EBITDA rose 32.9%, while the reported 46.2% gross margin included about 185 basis points from the tariff refund. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20; CIQ Financials Quarterly workbook, Q2 FY2026] |
| revenue-drivers | New-store rollout is the largest revenue driver and is improving. | New and non-comparable stores contributed $254.8 million, or 9.4 percentage points, of Q2 growth; the bridge has a 0.0-point residual. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales] |
| margin-drivers | Planned tariff-refund reinvestment is the largest known H2 margin mover. | Management guides Q3 adjusted EBIT margin down 60–80 basis points and Q4 down 40–60 basis points as it reinvests the refund; the Q2 underlying bridge reconciles with a negative 30-basis-point residual. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] |
| guidance-consensus | **Bar assessment: Fair.** | Q3 revenue consensus is 0.37% above the guidance midpoint and inside the range; normalized EPS is not definition-matched to company Adjusted EPS. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Consensus sheet, CIQ FQ3 2027, latest logged change 2026-09-22; Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook] |
| beat-miss-setup | **Setup is balanced.** | A beat needs continued store ramp, better mature-store demand and price investment without extra markdowns; weak traffic or weather can hurt sales and margin together. [Beat / Miss Setup, Sections 2–3, 8–10] |
| earnings-quality | **73/100 — mostly clean, with working-capital and adjustment noise.** | FY2025 cash from operations was 99.2% of CIQ-standard EBITDA, but reported trailing FCF of $412.5 million includes up to $55.5 million of non-recurring refund cash benefit. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.20, 30] |
| earnings-sensitivity | **58/100 — moderate volatility; higher is worse.** | A repeat or reversal of the 70-basis-point merchandise-margin contribution changes a Q3-like adjusted-EBITDA read by about $20.9 million under a zero-mitigation bound. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks; Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 2–4] |
| earnings-red-flags | **Material concerns.** | Eleven flags fired, including seven High flags; the central risk is a weak transaction response to H2 price investment, not fraud or a historical cash-conversion breakdown. [Earnings Red Flags, Sections 3–6] |

## 3. Reconciliation

No material disagreements between specialists. The apparent conflicts below are different metrics or bases, and they reconcile as follows.

| Apparent Conflict | Evidence On Each Side | Reconciled View |
|---|---|---|
| Q2 growth looks faster, while the annual trend is slower. | Q2 net sales grew 11.0%; annual growth slowed from 11.8% in FY2023 to 9.4% in FY2024 and 8.8% in FY2025. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.43; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.3] | Q2 total sales accelerated, but 9.4 of 11.0 percentage points came from new and non-comparable stores. This supports capacity-led growth, not proven mature-store demand acceleration. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales] |
| Reported gross margin improved 242 basis points, while H2 margin guidance falls. | Q2 reported gross margin was 46.2%, up 242 basis points; the $55.5 million refund supplied about 185 points. Management will reinvest it and guides H2 quarterly margin lower. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] | The filing-based headline is correct, but it is not recurring. Refund-excluded gross margin was 44.3%, up 60 basis points, and is the better starting point for H2. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] |
| CIQ and filing-derived EBITDA differ. | CIQ reports $1,360.7 million of trailing EBITDA; the filing-derived GAAP calculation is $1,440.2 million, a $79.5 million gap, including a roughly $54.0 million Q2 difference. [CIQ Financials, LTM Aug. 1, 2026; Historical Financials, Section 2] | The measures are not interchangeable. The refund is close to the Q2 gap, but the workbook gives no bridge; each EBITDA figure keeps its source and definition. |
| Management says gross margin rose about 250 basis points; the line-item calculation gives 242. | Management rounded the change; reported cost-of-sales and sales line items calculate to 242 basis points. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20] | Use 242 basis points for arithmetic and treat 250 as management’s rounded description; direction is unchanged. |

The red-flag agent’s **Material concerns** verdict is consistent with, rather than contrary to, the **Mixed earnings setup** verdict.

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No quarterly data | N | Earnings clarity | Not applied; max 60 unused |
| No consensus / estimate data | N | Consensus setup | Not applied; max 30 unused |

| No revision history | N | Consensus setup | Not applied; max 60 unused |
| No verbatim transcript AND no sell-side proxy | N | Earnings clarity | Not applied; max 70 unused |
| Transcript role filled ONLY by a sell-side proxy (no verbatim) | N | Earnings clarity | Not applied; max 70 unused |
| No segment-level P&L for a multi-segment business | N | Earnings clarity | Burlington is a single reportable segment; max 70 unused |
| Only inferred sensitivities | N | Earnings volatility confidence | No hard cap; operating-variable confidence remains limited, but a company-disclosed interest coefficient and management-reported historical margin moves exist |
| Conflicting sources not reconcilable | N | Overall usefulness | Not applied; max 65 unused because EBITDA differences are definition-labelled rather than merged |

## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

The current total-sales trajectory can continue while the store programme adds capacity, but it is capital-dependent rather than a one-time M&A, foreign-exchange or accounting effect. The reported-versus-underlying gap is material: new and non-comparable stores supplied 9.4 percentage points of Q2’s 11.0% growth, while comparable stores supplied 1.6 points. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales] The single factor that would flip the revenue direction is mature-store traffic: transactions were relatively flat in Q2, so weaker Fall visits could overwhelm the benefit from a larger store base. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A] The one-time H2 value investment may help traffic, but its sales response is not quantified and should not be treated as recurring growth. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]

### Margin Setup

Q2’s 46.2% reported gross margin is not sustainable as a run rate because about 185 basis points came from the refund; the better current anchor is the 44.3% refund-excluded margin, up 60 basis points year on year. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] This is a mid-cycle, not proven peak-or-trough, margin read because H2 has the planned reinvestment, seasonal weather risk and a larger holiday quarter still ahead. Burlington has one segment and no category profit disclosure, so a 10%–20% adverse move in any segment cannot be measured; the largest supportable operating test is instead a 70-basis-point merchandise-margin reversal, which would reduce Q3-like adjusted EBITDA by about $20.9 million under the specialist’s zero-mitigation bound. [Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 2–4] No contractual merchandise-cost pass-through or quantified realised offset is proven, although flexible sourcing, pricing, reserve inventory and supply-chain actions provide partial but unmeasured mitigation. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1—Sourcing and Merchandising Model; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]

### Quality Check

The largest gap between reported and economic earnings is the non-recurring $55.5 million refund: reported trailing FCF was $412.5 million, versus about $357.0 million after a conservative full-refund normalisation; whether that gap narrows cannot be proven until the H2 cash timing is reported. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.20, 30; Earnings Quality, Section 1] Lease, impairment and litigation adjustments recur, but the FY2025 adjusted-versus-GAAP net-income gap was only 2.5%. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] A next-year model should start from GAAP earnings, remove the tariff refund and assess recurring adjustments individually rather than use non-GAAP earnings as a blanket replacement.

### Consensus Bar

A material Q3 beat requires several linked outcomes: continued store ramp, mature-store sales near or above management’s range, and less margin loss than planned from the value investment. [Beat / Miss Setup, Sections 2–4] The revenue bar appears correctly set rather than low: it is 0.37% above management’s midpoint but inside the range, while the apparent EPS gap cannot be judged because CIQ normalized EPS and company Adjusted EPS are not definition-matched. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Consensus sheet, CIQ FQ3 2027, latest logged change 2026-09-22; Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook] The latest Q2 surprise was helped by the refund, but Q3 normalized EPS was reset from $2.04 to $1.73 and the degree to which consensus still relies on that one-off is not measurable. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Trends sheet, CIQ FQ3 2027, latest logged change 2026-09-22]

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

Leverage is within normal range and did not change materially during the period — no dedicated treatment required.

## 6. Key Numbers

- Revenue growth rate: Q2 FY2026 net sales were $2,997.8 million, up 11.0%; 9.4 percentage points came from new and non-comparable stores and 1.6 points from comparable stores. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.3 and MD&A—Net Sales]
- EBITDA margin: CIQ-standard trailing EBITDA was $1,360.7 million, or 11.0% of sales; it is a vendor calculation, not a filing-reported or company-adjusted measure. [CIQ Financials, LTM Aug. 1, 2026]
- EPS: Q2 GAAP diluted EPS was $2.88, including about $0.64 from the tariff refund. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.3; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]
- CFO / EBITDA: FY2025 cash from operations was 99.2% of CIQ-standard EBITDA; reported trailing FCF was $412.5 million and the conservative refund-normalised read was about $357.0 million. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; CIQ Financials Annual workbook; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20]
- Biggest driver current level: 1,287 stores at Q2 end, up 149 net over the trailing year; recent and non-comparable stores added $254.8 million of Q2 sales. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A]
- Consensus gap: Q3 revenue consensus of $2,992.38 million is $10.90 million, or 0.37%, above the guidance midpoint and remains inside the range; the EPS gap is not assessable on a matched basis. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Consensus sheet, CIQ FQ3 2027, latest logged change 2026-09-22]
- Estimate revision direction: Q3 normalized EPS fell from $2.04 at 60/90 days ago to $1.73, while Q3 revenue stayed near $2,992 million. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Trends sheet, CIQ FQ3 2027, latest logged change 2026-09-22]
- Earnings volatility score: 58/100, where higher is worse; merchandise margin is the largest supportable two-sided variable at about $20.9 million of Q3-like adjusted EBITDA for a 70-basis-point move under a zero-mitigation bound. [Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 2–4, 7]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mixed earnings setup | Q3 shows that transactions, not only basket and new stores, are improving; refund-excluded merchandise margin holds; and the Q4 outlook shows that the larger holiday quarter can absorb the remaining price investment. | Mature-store transactions weaken, inventory requires more markdowns, refund-excluded margin gives back its gain, or management cuts its full-year sales or earnings range. | The highest-value item is the Q3 transaction response to the planned value investment, reported with the basket split and refund-excluded margin bridge. |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Dominant trend and driver:** The setup is mixed. Total sales and underlying margin improved, but most Q2 growth came from store capacity rather than mature-store traffic. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales]
- **Cash backing:** Historical earnings are cash-backed, but the latest reported cash read must be reduced for up to $55.5 million of non-recurring refund benefit; several adjusted items also recur. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.29, 45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.20, 30]
- **Consensus bar:** Revenue is fairly set inside guidance; the EPS bar is not cleanly comparable because vendor normalized EPS and company Adjusted EPS use unmatched definitions. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Consensus sheet, latest logged change 2026-09-22; Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook]
- **Next-quarter and look-ahead:** Q3 is balanced, but even a Q3 beat will not settle Q4, which has averaged 31.5% of annual revenue and carries about $33 million of the planned value investment. [CIQ Financials Quarterly workbook, FY2023–FY2025; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]
- **Top sensitivity:** Merchandise margin improved 70 basis points in Q2; a reversal is the largest supportable two-sided operating sensitivity, while its durability is unproven. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks; Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 2–4]
- **Partial-data caps:** None of the formal caps applies. Missing price elasticity, store-cohort returns and operating coefficients still limit precision, especially on the downside.
- **Red-flag severity verdict: Material concerns.**
- **High flag — capacity-led growth:** About 86% of Q2’s dollar sales increase came from new and non-comparable stores while mature-store transactions were relatively flat. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A]
- **High flag — reported margin is not recurring:** The $55.5 million Q2 tariff refund will be reinvested in H2, so the reported Q2 margin cannot be extrapolated. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]
- **High flag — Q3 upside is conjunctive:** A beat needs store ramp, mature-store demand and price-investment conversion to work together; weak traffic or weather creates the simpler miss path. [Beat / Miss Setup, Sections 2–3]
- **High flag — Q4 remains unresolved:** Q4 is the larger seasonal quarter and carries roughly 60% of the planned refund reinvestment, so a Q3 beat alone cannot upgrade the setup. [Beat / Miss Setup, Sections 5–6, 9]
- **High flag — latest cash quality is inflated:** Reported trailing FCF includes up to the $55.5 million refund cash benefit; the normalised read is about $357.0 million versus $412.5 million reported. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.20, 30; Earnings Quality, Section 1]
- **High flag — correlated downside is unquantified:** Demand, weather, markdown and selling-cost leverage can worsen together, but the company discloses no operating coefficients for that chain. [Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 1–2, 5–7]
- **High flag — acceleration framing is too strong:** Capacity-led growth, flat mature-store transactions and refund-aided reported results support a mixed verdict, not proven earnings acceleration. [Revenue Drivers, Sections 4, 6–7; Margin Drivers, Sections 3, 8]
- **RF-EQ-001 (rising accruals divergent from cash earnings)**
- **Biggest missing data point:** The transaction response to the Q3 value investment; without it, price elasticity remains unproven.
- **What changes the verdict:** Upgrade only when transaction-led mature-store demand and refund-excluded margin hold through the larger Q4; downgrade on weaker transactions, markdown pressure and a full-year guidance cut.

## 9. Simple Summary

- Q2 sales grew 11%, but about 86% of the dollar increase came from new and non-comparable stores. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Net Sales]
- Underlying margin improved, but the reported Q2 margin included a $55.5 million refund that will be reinvested. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks]
- Earnings are mostly cash-backed; the latest trailing cash figure needs a refund adjustment. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.30]
- The consensus bar is fair, not obviously easy, and the EPS definitions do not match cleanly. [Capital IQ Estimates Report, Consensus sheet, latest logged change 2026-09-22; Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook]
- The next-quarter setup is balanced.
- Merchandise margin and markdown execution are the largest measurable operating sensitivity. [Earnings Sensitivity, Sections 2–4]
- Earnings volatility is moderate, with correlated weather, traffic and markdown risk that cannot be sized precisely.
- This module is useful for the master synthesizer, but it supports a mixed setup rather than an acceleration call.

## earnings / 01_historical-financials.md

_Source: `earnings/01_historical-financials.md`_

# Historical Financials — BURL

Burlington reports under U.S. GAAP in USD and uses a January fiscal year-end. This report uses the company's fiscal-year labels: FY2025 ended January 31, 2026; FY2023 had 53 weeks. Amounts below are USD millions except per-share data, percentages, and multiples. “Revenue” means reported net sales, not the small other-revenue line. Gross profit is net sales less cost of sales. Free cash flow (FCF, cash left after investment) is cash from operations (CFO) less the reported `cash paid for property and equipment` capex line, consistently throughout.

EBIT and EBITDA are not GAAP subtotals reported by Burlington. To keep the multi-year and quarterly series consistent, those two rows use the source-bound Capital IQ standard calculation, labelled as such; company-reported adjusted measures are separated in Section 4. Filing-based checks and the CIQ reconciliation are stated below rather than treating unlike definitions as interchangeable.

## 1. Annual Financial Table (4 years)

**USD millions except EPS, percentages, and multiples; GAAP unless labelled CIQ standard.** FY2023 had 53 weeks, so its growth rate has one extra week of trading versus the 52-week years.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 (53 weeks) | FY2024 | FY2025 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Revenue — net sales [1][2] | 8,684.5 | 9,709.0 | 10,616.7 | 11,549.6 | Decelerating |
| Revenue YoY % [1][2] | N/A | 11.8% | 9.4% | 8.8% | Decelerating |
| Gross Profit — net sales less cost of sales [1][2] | 3,512.8 | 4,124.9 | 4,591.5 | 5,062.7 | Decelerating |
| Gross Margin % [1][2] | 40.5% | 42.5% | 43.2% | 43.8% | Decelerating |
| EBITDA — CIQ standard calculation [5] | 650.9 | 847.4 | 1,048.1 | 1,241.5 | Decelerating |
| EBITDA Margin % — CIQ standard [5] | 7.5% | 8.7% | 9.9% | 10.7% | Decelerating |
| EBIT — CIQ operating-income calculation [5] | 401.7 | 563.3 | 726.2 | 864.3 | Decelerating |
| EBIT Margin % — CIQ standard [5] | 4.6% | 5.8% | 6.8% | 7.5% | Decelerating |
| EPS (diluted, GAAP) [1][2] | 3.49 | 5.23 | 7.80 | 9.51 | Decelerating |
| CFO [1][2] | 596.4 | 868.7 | 863.4 | 1,231.4 | Volatile |
| Capex — cash paid for property and equipment [1][2] | 447.4 | 492.6 | 880.4 | 1,059.8 | Volatile |
| FCF (CFO − capex) [1][2] | 149.0 | 376.1 | (17.0) | 171.6 | Volatile |
| Working Capital — current assets − current liabilities [1][2][4] | 371.8 | 298.2 | 356.3 | 522.3 | Volatile |
| Net Debt — **strict basis** [1][2][4] | 603.1* | 483.3 | 716.1 | 849.8 | Volatile |
| Net Debt / EBITDA — same **strict** basis [1][2][4][5] | 0.93x* | 0.57x | 0.68x | 0.68x | Stable |

*FY2022 strict net debt is `$13.6m` current debt + `$1,462.1m` long-term debt − `$872.6m` cash = `$603.1m`, from CIQ balance-sheet components that separately show operating leases; composition is not cross-checked to the FY2022 filing debt note because that filing is not in the frozen pool. FY2023–FY2025 strict net debt is filing-based: current maturities plus long-term debt, excluding the separately stated operating-lease liabilities, less cash. The balance-sheet build is therefore visible rather than using CIQ's lease-inclusive “Total Debt.”

**Annual reading.** Net sales rose every year, but the annual growth rate slowed from 11.8% in FY2023 to 8.8% in FY2025; the FY2023 comparison also had a 53rd week. Gross margin increased 334 basis points from FY2022 to FY2025 and CIQ-standard EBITDA margin rose 325 basis points. Cash generation did not move in a straight line: FY2024 CFO was flat while capex rose to `$880.4m`, turning FCF slightly negative; FY2025 CFO rose to `$1,231.4m` and FCF recovered to `$171.6m`. [FY2024 Form 10-K, pp.50, 53; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.43, 46; CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Income Statement and Cash Flow]

## 2. TTM Snapshot

| Metric | Latest TTM (to Aug. 1, 2026) | Prior TTM (to Aug. 2, 2025) | Change | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Revenue — net sales | 12,198.6 | 10,999.3 | +10.9% | [3][5] |
| EBITDA — CIQ standard calculation | 1,360.7 | 1,113.4 | +22.2% | [5][6] |
| EBIT — CIQ operating-income calculation | 951.6 | 773.6 | +23.0% | [5] |
| EPS diluted — CIQ LTM / standalone-quarter sum | 11.13 | 8.47 | +31.4% | [5] |
| CFO | 1,415.5 | 804.1 | +76.0% | [2][3][5] |
| Capex — cash paid for property and equipment | 1,002.9 | 1,109.1 | (9.6%) | [2][3][5] |
| FCF (CFO − capex) | 412.5 | (305.0) | Inflected positive | [2][3][5] |
| Net debt at latest period-end — **strict basis** | 1,209.9 | 1,291.7 | (81.8) | [3] |

*Net debt is a point-in-time balance-sheet metric, not a TTM flow.* Latest strict net debt is `$20.1m` current debt + `$1,893.4m` long-term debt − `$703.7m` cash = `$1,209.9m`; the same-date prior amount is `$19.9m + $2,019.4m − $747.6m = $1,291.7m`. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5]

**CIQ-sidecar reconciliation.** The required source-bound sidecar reports CIQ LTM EBITDA of `$1,360.7m` and CIQ net debt of `$5,202.4m` at August 1, 2026. The latter is not strict net debt: its `$5,906.1m` debt total includes `$3,992.6m` of operating-lease liabilities (`$448.7m` current + `$3,543.9m` long term), whereas the filing-strict debt build above excludes them. [CIQ Financials→Balance Sheet and Income Statement, Q2/LTM Aug. 1, 2026; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5]

For a filing-based cross-check, four-quarter GAAP EBITDA calculated from the filings is `$1,440.2m`, or `$79.5m` above CIQ's `$1,360.7m`. Q2 FY2026 alone is `$369.7m` on that filing calculation versus CIQ's `$315.6m`, a `$54.0m` difference. The 10-Q identifies a `$55.5m` tariff refund in Q2 cost of sales; that is close to, but does not by itself prove the cause of, the CIQ difference, leaving a `$1.5m` classification/rounding residual. The CIQ workbook does not disclose a bridge, so these figures are not interchangeable. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20; CIQ Financials Quarterly workbook; CIQ facts sidecar]

## 3. Latest Quarterly Trend Table (8 quarters)

**USD millions except EPS and percentages.** Q4 values are actual quarterly CIQ columns, not annual figures divided by four. EBITDA is the CIQ standard calculation so each quarterly value rolls to its CIQ annual and LTM counterpart. Revenue, gross margin, and EPS for Q1/Q2 FY2026 have been cross-checked to the 10-Q; earlier quarters use the frozen CIQ filed-quarter archive where the underlying 10-Qs are not in the pool.

The company states that Q2 FY2026 gross margin was 46.2% versus 43.7% a year earlier, rounded as a 250-basis-point improvement. Using the reported line items in the table gives a 242-basis-point improvement. The `$55.5m` tariff refund equals roughly 185 basis points of Q2 net sales (`55.5 ÷ 2,997.8`), leaving 57 basis points of the line-item margin change; the filing attributes the remaining improvement qualitatively to merchandise margin, not to a quantified recurring driver. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20]

## 4. Reported vs Adjusted Metrics

The company does not report a GAAP EBITDA or GAAP EBIT subtotal. “Reported” below is a filing-derived GAAP calculation: net income + interest expense − interest income + tax + D&A for EBITDA, and the same calculation without D&A for EBIT. It is not the CIQ standard measure in Sections 1–3.

| EBIT | 866.3 (GAAP calculation) | 887.1 | +20.8 | Same pre-D&A reconciliation items. | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| EPS (diluted) | 9.51 | 9.76 | +0.25 | Company tax-effects its stated adjustment set. | [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.29, 43] |

## 5. Quarterly Seasonality Table (last 3 fiscal years)

**Revenue shares use reported net sales. EBITDA margins use the reconciled CIQ standard quarterly series, not company adjusted EBITDA.** Q4 consistently exceeds 30% of annual revenue and is therefore the key seasonal quarter.

| Quarter | FY2023 Rev Share | FY2024 Rev Share | FY2025 Rev Share | Avg Rev Share | FY2023 EBITDA Margin | FY2024 EBITDA Margin | FY2025 EBITDA Margin |

## 6. Key Trend Summary

Annual revenue growth has slowed from 11.8% in FY2023 to 8.8% in FY2025, although latest Q2 FY2026 net sales were still up 11.0% year on year. Margins have expanded across the annual record: gross margin rose from 40.5% in FY2022 to 43.8% in FY2025 and CIQ-standard EBITDA margin rose from 7.5% to 10.7%; the Q2 FY2026 gross-margin print of 46.2% is not a normalised run rate because the filing includes a `$55.5m` tariff refund. Seasonality is material: Q4 supplied an average 31.5% of annual sales in FY2023–FY2025 and its EBITDA margin ranged from 12.4% to 14.2%, above the first three quarters. FCF moved from `(17.0)m` in FY2024 to `$171.6m` in FY2025 and `$412.5m` over the latest TTM, while latest strict net debt was `$1,209.9m`, below the `$1,291.7m` same-date prior strict balance but above the FY2025 year-end **strict net-debt** balance of `$849.8m`. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.43, 45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 5, 20]

# Revenue Drivers — BURL

Burlington reports under U.S. GAAP in USD. Its fiscal year ends on the Saturday closest to January 31; the latest reported quarter is Q2 FY2026, ended August 1, 2026. “Sales” below means net sales unless noted otherwise.

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Single-segment business (>85% from one segment) — consolidated analysis.

Burlington has one U.S. off-price retail segment, which supplied 100% of FY2025 reported revenue. The FY2025 10-K reports total revenue of $11,566.9m for that segment. The frozen CIQ facts sidecar reads `Retail - Apparel` revenue of $11,559m (100%); the $7.9m (0.07%) difference is a vendor-versus-filing definition/extraction difference, so the filing figure governs. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 1—Segment Information; CIQ Financials→Segments, 12 months Jan-31-2026—vendor export]

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

| Business Type | Revenue Formula |
|---|---|
| Retail | Store count × sales per store |

Company-specific formula: **net sales = operating Burlington stores × net sales per store; comparable-store sales = customer transactions × average basket.** More than 99% of FY2025 net sales came from Burlington stores. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1—Our Stores; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Q&A]

The retail overlay's sales-per-square-foot and numerical inventory-turn KPIs are absent from the admitted pool. The company discloses store count and comparable-store sales, but not either KPI, so a more granular productivity bridge is not proven from available data. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 2—Properties; Item 1—Our Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model]

## 3. Market / Share / Price / Mix Split

| Driver Bucket | Current Direction | Evidence | Importance /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| End-market demand | Mixed: Q2 mature-store demand grew, but only through basket; traffic was flat. Lower-income trade areas outperformed the chain, while management described shoppers as under pressure. | Q2 comparable-store sales rose 2% after 5% a year earlier; basket was the main contributor and transactions were relatively flat. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks and Q&A] | 80 |
| Company market share | Unknown. New sites add selling capacity, but the company does not disclose a market-share series. Store rollout is company execution, not proof of share gain. | 149 net stores were added in the trailing 12 months, a 13% increase in store count. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] | 70 |
| Price / realization | Lower intended customer prices in H2 FY2026. This may support demand, but the sales elasticity is not disclosed. | The company plans to reinvest the $55m Q2 tariff refund in sharper values, about 40% in Q3 and 60% in Q4. [BURL Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, prepared remarks] | 50 |
| Product / customer / geography mix | Improving but unquantified. Beauty and accessories were the strongest categories and Home began to outperform; no category revenue shares are disclosed. | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] | 35 |
| FX translation | No material direct revenue translation identified. Burlington reports one U.S. segment; overseas sourcing is a cost risk, not a disclosed revenue-translation driver. | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1—Segment Reporting; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A—International Operations] | 5 |
| M&A / divestitures | No contribution disclosed. The Q2 filing attributes the sales increase entirely to comparable and new/non-comparable stores. | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)] | 5 |

## 4. Revenue Driver Table (consolidated)

| Driver | Current Level | Direction (Improving / Stable / Deteriorating / Unknown) | Magnitude (High / Mid / Low) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Store rollout / selling capacity | 1,287 stores at Q2 end; 149 net stores added in the trailing 12 months (+13%). Management guides to about 115 net new stores in FY2026. | Improving | High | Q2 sales bridge assigns $254.8m of the $296.8m increase to the 149 net new and non-comparable stores. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales); BURL Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook] |
| Mature-store demand | Comparable-store sales +2% in Q2, following +5% a year earlier; the two-year stack was +7%. Basket rose while transactions were relatively flat. | Improving, but slower | Mid | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks and Q&A] |
| Merchandise availability, assortment and value | Comparable-store inventory was +11% year on year; reserve inventory was 43% of total inventory, down from 50%. Beauty/accessories were strongest and Home began to outperform. | Improving | Mid | [BURL Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Fiscal 2026 Second Quarter Operating Results; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |
| Tariff-refund price investment | $55m Q2 tariff refund is being spent on lower prices in H2, rather than retained as earnings. The direct sales effect is not quantified. | Improving for value, unknown for sales | Low | [BURL Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| Weather and outerwear demand | Late-September onward weather is an important driver of Q3 comparable sales; warmer Fall weather would weigh on outerwear demand. | Unknown | Mid (qualitative; no filed sensitivity) | [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1—Seasonality; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |
| Low-income consumer spending / traffic | Lower-income trade areas continued to grow comparable sales faster than the chain, but management cited higher gas prices and pressure on shoppers. | Mixed | Mid | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |

**Cycle position: Mid-cycle (inference, not from filings).** Q2 total sales grew 11%, while the reported mature-store comparable-sales metric was +2%, and FY2023–FY2025 annual net-sales growth slowed from 11.8% to 8.8%. That evidence does not establish a demand peak or a trough. The coming Fall is not a clean run-rate test: management plans to use a one-time $55m tariff refund to lower prices in Q3/Q4 and will lap prior-year weather disruption in Q3 and tariff-related supply constraints in Q3/Q4. The refund investment is a one-time policy-related price investment with possible sales support, not a recurring demand driver. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7—Results of Operations; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

## 5. Revenue Drivers By Segment (if applicable)

### Segment: U.S. off-price retail (100% of FY2025 revenue)

| Driver | Current Level | Direction | Magnitude | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New and non-comparable stores | 149 net stores added since Q2 FY2025; 1,287 stores at Q2 FY2026 end. | Improving | High | $254.8m of Q2 sales growth came from this source. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)] |
| Comparable-store sales | +2% Q2; primarily basket, with transactions relatively flat. | Improving, but slower | Mid | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |
| Assortment / value | Beauty and accessories led category trends; Home started to outperform. Planned H2 price investment may strengthen the value offer, but its effect is not quantified. | Improving, unquantified | Mid | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |
| Weather | Outerwear sales remain sensitive to Fall temperature; management has shifted planning toward more weather-neutral product and regional localization. | Unknown | Mid (qualitative) | [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1—Seasonality; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |

Product-category, channel and store-cohort revenue or profit disclosures are not available, so this segment cannot be decomposed further without inventing mix weights. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 1—Segment Information]

## 6. Revenue Growth Decomposition

Q2 FY2026 net sales increased $296.8m to $2,997.8m, or 11.0%, from Q2 FY2025. The filing gives a complete dollar bridge: $254.8m from 149 net new and non-comparable stores, plus $42.0m from comparable stores. The $42.0m comparable-store amount was driven mainly by a higher basket, but the call does not split it into price, mix and transaction dollars. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales); Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A]

| Component | Contribution to Growth (pp) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| New and non-comparable stores (capacity / volume) | +9.4 | Reported $254.8m ÷ Q2 FY2025 net sales of $2,701.0m. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)] |
| Comparable stores (mainly basket; transaction / price / mix split unavailable) | +1.6 | Reported $42.0m ÷ Q2 FY2025 net sales of $2,701.0m; transactions were relatively flat. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales); Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, Q&A] |
| FX, M&A and other | 0.0 residual | The filing's two reported components sum to the full $296.8m increase. This is not a separate claim that FX or M&A exposure is zero. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)] |
| Total net-sales growth | +11.0 | $2,997.8m versus $2,701.0m. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Consolidated Statements of Income; MD&A—Results of Operations] |

## 6a. Decomposition Attribution and Residual (MODULE_RULES "Driver Attribution" / §15)

**New and non-comparable stores:** reported $254.8m contribution ÷ $2,701.0m Q2 FY2025 net-sales base [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)]
  = **9.43pp** of the 10.99pp observed growth
  → Asserted from disclosure, no volume/price/mix ratio applied. Basis matches: the component and total are both divided by the same prior-year quarterly net-sales base.

**Comparable stores:** reported $42.0m contribution ÷ $2,701.0m Q2 FY2025 net-sales base [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales)]
  = **1.55pp** of the 10.99pp observed growth
  → Asserted from disclosure, no basket, price or mix ratio applied. The transcript identifies higher basket and flat transactions, but gives no ratio that can allocate the $42.0m further. Basis matches: the same prior-year quarterly net-sales base is used.

Reconciliation: $254.8m + $42.0m = $296.8m. On the common Q2 FY2025 sales base, 9.43pp + 1.55pp = 10.99pp versus reported total growth of 10.99pp; **10.99pp reconciled, 0.00pp residual** before rounding. The bridge therefore supports a new-store conclusion, while it does not support a separate price/mix contribution claim.

RF-EARN-001: revenue decomposition reconciled — explained 11.0pp, residual 0.0pp, total 11.0pp

## 7. The Single Biggest Revenue Driver

**New-store rollout is the single biggest revenue driver, and it is improving.** In Q2, recent and non-comparable stores supplied $254.8m of the $296.8m sales increase—9.4pp of the reported 11.0% growth, or about 86% of the dollar increase—so it clears the roughly half-of-growth test. The rollout is still active: trailing-12-month net store count grew 13% to 1,287 and management guides to about 115 net new FY2026 stores. The important qualification is that mature-store demand was only +2%, driven mainly by basket while transactions were flat; weaker traffic, warm Fall weather, or a smaller-than-expected response to H2 price investment would therefore reduce the benefit from the larger store base. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A—Results of Operations (Net sales); BURL Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Outlook; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks and Q&A]
