# Margin Drivers — BURL

Burlington reports under U.S. GAAP in USD. Fiscal 2026 ends January 30, 2027; the latest reported period is Q2 FY2026, the 13 weeks ended August 1, 2026. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Fiscal Year]

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Business-model inputs are available. Burlington has one U.S. off-price retail reportable segment, representing 100% of FY2025 revenue and profit. It does not disclose margins by merchandise category, store cohort, or channel, so this is a consolidated analysis; a product-category margin split is not assessable from the filings. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 1 — Segment Information; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Segment Reporting]

Sector overlay applied: Retail / consumer — margin analysis uses comparable-store sales, gross margin, inventory/reserve mix, store rollout, and product-sourcing/SG&A leverage. Sales per square foot and numerical inventory turns are not disclosed. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Business and Our Off-Price Sourcing and Merchandising Model; frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md, Retail / consumer row]

**Cycle position: mid-cycle, not a normalised margin run rate.** This is an inference, not from filings: Q2 comparable-store sales were +2% after +5% a year earlier, while the reported 46.2% gross margin includes a +185 bps tariff-refund effect that management will reinvest in the second half. The business is seasonally weighted to back-to-school and holiday demand, and management identifies weather and low-income consumer spending as material variables. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Comparable Store Sales and Gross Margin; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1 — Seasonality]

## 2. Cost Stack

| Retail cost / margin KPI | Latest reading | Direction | Evidence | Margin risk |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Comparable-store sales (SSSG) | +2% in Q2 FY2026; +7% two-year stack | Slower versus +5% Q2 FY2025 | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] | Traffic and basket softness would reduce fixed-cost absorption; no bps sensitivity is disclosed. |
| Gross margin / cost of sales | 46.2% / 53.8%; 44.3% gross margin excluding the refund | Reported improvement is non-recurring | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin and Results of Operations] | The $55.5m refund reduced cost of sales; its reinvestment makes the reported level non-run-rate. |
| Merchandise margin | +70 bps in Q2, excluding tariff refunds | Tailwind | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] | Markdowns or weaker buying availability would reverse the main underlying Q2 driver. |
| Freight | +10 bps expense in Q2, excluding tariff refunds | Headwind | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] | Inbound and distribution-centre freight is in cost of sales, but the filing gives no dollar or rate sensitivity. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin] |
| Product sourcing costs | $225.9m, 7.5% of sales, down 20 bps YoY | Tailwind | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Segment Reporting; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin] | Savings rely on supply-chain efficiency initiatives; the filing does not split freight, labour and technology components. |
| SG&A | $1,019.2m, 34.0% of sales, down about 117 bps from 35.2% | Tailwind | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 26–27] | Better occupancy, selling supplies, legal reserve and product-sourcing costs helped; 149 net new stores still raised dollar SG&A 7.3%. |
| Labour | Not disclosed separately; store payroll is within other segment expenses | Unknown | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Segment Reporting] | The company has raised hourly wages annually since 2010 and identifies wage/benefit pressure as a risk, but it gives no labour-cost sensitivity. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A — Labour costs] |
| Energy | Not disclosed separately | Unknown | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Segment Reporting] | Not proven from available data. |
| D&A | $114.0m, 3.8% of sales, up about 29 bps YoY | Headwind | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 27] | New/non-comparable stores and supply-chain infrastructure raised D&A. |
| Inventory / reserve mix | Inventory $1,541.3m, +8.9% YoY; comparable-store inventory +11%; reserve 43% of inventory versus 50% | Mixed | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Inventory] | More inventory can support chasing sales; it can also lead to markdowns if demand or weather disappoints. A numerical turn is not disclosed. |
| Interest expense | $19.7m, 0.7% of sales, roughly flat as a rate | Neutral | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.3] | It affects earnings after EBIT, not operating margin. |

Cost of sales includes merchandise net of purchase discounts and allowances, inbound and distribution-centre outbound freight, commissions and import fees. Store payroll and several selling costs sit outside cost of sales, so a retailer comparison using only COGS would miss material operating costs. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin]

## 3. Gross Margin → EBITDA Margin → EBIT Margin Walk

**Q2 FY2026 versus Q2 FY2025; USD millions.** Gross margin is GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBIT are company-defined non-GAAP measures and include the Q2 tariff refund in the reconciliation; they are not interchangeable with a GAAP operating-income subtotal.

| Margin Level | Latest | Prior Year | Change bps | Main Reason | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin (GAAP) | 46.2% | 43.7% | +242 | $55.5m tariff refunds plus improved merchandise margin | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20, MD&A — Gross Margin] |
| Adjusted EBITDA margin (company-defined) | 12.5% ($375.3m) | 9.1% ($245.7m) | +342 | Gross-margin lift and expense leverage; includes the refund | [Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures] |
| Adjusted EBIT margin (company-defined) | 8.7% ($261.3m) | 5.6% ($150.9m) | +313 | Same factors, less D&A; includes the refund | [Q2 FY2026 earnings release, Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures] |

The reported gross-margin change calculates to +242 bps: `(2,997.778 − 1,614.011) ÷ 2,997.778 = 46.160%` versus `(2,701.026 − 1,519.629) ÷ 2,701.026 = 43.739%`. The refund alone was `$55.5m ÷ $2,997.8m = 1.851%`, or +185 bps, leaving +57 bps not separately allocated by the filing; the filing attributes that residual qualitatively to merchandise margin. This is not a realised price pass-through measure. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20, MD&A — Gross Margin]

Management's underlying Q2 view removes the refund and bankruptcy-acquired-lease costs: gross margin was 44.3%, up 60 bps; adjusted EBIT margin rose 100 bps to about 7%. Management attributes the underlying gross-margin change to +70 bps merchandise margin partly offset by +10 bps freight. It expects the tariff-refund effect to be neutral for the full year because it will reinvest the refund into customer value in Q3 and Q4. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

**CIQ basis reconciliation.** The required sidecar's authoritative vendor read is LTM EBITDA of $1,360.7m and an 11% LTM EBITDA margin through August 1, 2026. This is a CIQ standard LTM calculation, whereas the table is a company-defined, single-quarter adjusted measure; the two are therefore not interchangeable and are not a conflict with the filing-based quarterly walk. [CIQ Financials→Income Statement 'EBITDA' [LTM 12 months Aug-01-2026], ciq_facts.json; CIQ Financials→Income Statement margin % + absolute EBITDA reconciler, ciq_facts.json]

## 4. Margin Walk — Which Margin Level Matters Most?

Underlying adjusted EBIT margin matters most. Gross margin isolates buying, markdowns and freight, but it misses the operating leverage from 149 net new stores and the D&A increase from store and distribution-centre investment. Adjusted EBIT captures those effects and is the metric management guides: excluding planned refund reinvestment, its fall guidance assumed a 10–30 bps improvement. The measure is non-GAAP, so reported gross margin and the refund-adjusted bridge remain necessary checks. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

## 5. Margin Driver Table (consolidated)

| Driver | Impact on Margins | Direction (Tailwind / Neutral / Headwind / Unknown) | Magnitude (High / Mid / Low) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Merchandise margin / markdown execution | +70 bps in Q2 underlying gross margin; availability of discounted branded goods and markdown discipline determine whether it holds. | Tailwind | Mid | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A — Merchandise supply] |
| Freight | +10 bps Q2 cost pressure in the underlying gross-margin bridge. | Headwind | Low | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| Product-sourcing efficiency | +20 bps Q2 benefit from supply-chain initiatives. | Tailwind | Low | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Gross Margin] |

The magnitude labels use actual disclosed moves where available. For consumer demand and weather, “Mid” is an inference from their importance to sales and the second-half seasonal mix, not a company-disclosed margin sensitivity.

## 6. Margin Drivers By Segment (if applicable)

Not applicable. Burlington is a single reportable U.S. off-price retail segment. Product-category and store-cohort margins are not disclosed, so further segmentation would be invented. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 1 — Segment Information]

## 7. Margin Bridge — Latest Period

This is management's **underlying adjusted EBIT-margin bridge** for Q2 FY2026 versus Q2 FY2025. It excludes the tariff refund and bankruptcy-acquired-lease costs, matching the stated +100 bps total. It must not be combined with the +242 bps reported GAAP gross-margin change above, which has a different metric and tariff basis. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

| Component | Margin Impact (bps) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Merchandise margin (price / product mix) | +70 | Management-reported underlying gross-margin driver. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| Freight | (10) | Management-reported underlying gross-margin driver. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| Product sourcing / supply-chain efficiency | +20 | Product sourcing fell 20 bps of sales. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| SG&A / operating leverage | +50 | Adjusted SG&A fell 50 bps, helped by lower store-related costs and total-sales leverage. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |
| Tariff refund | 0 | Excluded by management from this underlying bridge; separately, it added about +185 bps to reported Q2 gross margin. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20] |
| Other, including D&A and unquantified items | (30) | Residual required to reconcile the disclosed +100 bps total; not a management-attributed driver. |
| **Total underlying adjusted EBIT-margin change** | **+100** | [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |

## 7a. Bridge Attribution and Residual (MODULE_RULES "Driver Attribution" / §15)

Merchandise margin: **Asserted from disclosure, no sensitivity applied** — management reported +70 bps on the Q2 underlying gross-margin basis. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

Freight: **Asserted from disclosure, no sensitivity applied** — management reported a 10 bps expense increase on the same Q2 underlying gross-margin basis. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

Product sourcing: **Asserted from disclosure, no sensitivity applied** — management reported +20 bps on Q2 sales; the 10-Q gives $225.9m versus $209.0m and confirms the initiative. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 1 — Segment Reporting]

SG&A / operating leverage: **Asserted from disclosure, no sensitivity applied** — management reported adjusted SG&A down 50 bps on Q2 sales. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

Other: `reported total +100 bps − (+70 − 10 + 20 + 50 bps) = −30 bps`. This is the residual, not an attribution. It can include the D&A step-up and other items management did not size within this bridge. The basis matches throughout: Q2 FY2026 versus Q2 FY2025, company-defined adjusted EBIT margin, both excluding tariff refunds and bankruptcy-acquired-lease costs.

Sum of specifically reported components = `+70 − 10 + 20 + 50 = +130 bps`; `+130 bps + (−30 bps residual) = +100 bps` total. The named merchandise-margin driver accounts for 70% of the +100 bps underlying move, so it clears the threshold for the largest disclosed Q2 component. The residual is still material and prevents a more granular causal claim.

RF-EARN-002: margin bridge reconciled — explained 130bps, residual -30bps, total 100bps

## 8. The Single Biggest Margin Driver

For the next two reported quarters, the planned tariff-refund reinvestment is the largest known mover of reported margin. Management says it will use about 40% of the refund in Q3 and 60% in Q4 to offer sharper value, and guides operating margin down 60–80 bps in Q3 and 40–60 bps in Q4 because of that choice. This is a deliberate, finite headwind rather than proof that underlying costs have worsened: excluding that reinvestment, management's fall adjusted-EBIT-margin assumption remains +10–30 bps. Within Q2's underlying bridge, merchandise margin is the largest disclosed component at +70 bps. [Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks]

## 9. Investment Spend — Both Signs

FY2025 capital expenditure was $1,104.1m, up from $843.9m in FY2024, so this section applies. The FY2025 total comprises $482.0m for stores, $464.0m for supply-chain initiatives, and the remainder for IT and other initiatives; it is an aggregate of different projects but all are capital spend in the same fiscal year. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7 — Capital Expenditures]

| Reading | What it would show | Evidence here |
|---|---|---|
| Spend as a future **cost** | Store and distribution-centre spend becomes D&A and can squeeze EBIT margin before revenue fully matures. | Q2 D&A was $114.0m, up from $94.8m; D&A rose from 3.5% to 3.8% of sales (+29 bps), mainly from new/non-comparable stores and supply-chain infrastructure. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 27] |
| Spend as a **demand signal** | Store growth should yield incremental sales and fixed-cost absorption. This is evidence from open stores, not contracted backlog. | The 149 net new stores opened since Q2 FY2025 produced $254.8m of Q2 net-sales growth; management reported 45 net new stores opened in Q2. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, MD&A — Results of Operations; Q2 FY2026 earnings call, 2026-08-27, prepared remarks] |

**Current read:** Both signs matter. The Q2 sales contribution from new stores supports the demand reading for store investment, while the D&A rise is already a measurable margin cost. The evidence does not prove that all supply-chain infrastructure will earn its cost, because Burlington gives no backlog or distribution-centre return disclosure. The observable that would flip the current read is store-led sales growth and adjusted EBIT margin failing to absorb the continuing D&A increase; a numerical threshold is not proven from available data.

Burlington's next filing is company Q3 FY2026, a standalone 13-week quarter ending 2026-10-31; Capital IQ's expected 2026-11-25 results date is a vendor calendar date, not company-confirmed, and the vendor also estimates $279.00m EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation). Q3 supplied an average 23.6% of annual sales in FY2023–FY2025, below Q4's 31.5% but still exposed to the Fall selling season; management guides Q3 total sales up 9%–11%, comparable-store sales (mature-store sales versus the same stores a year ago) up 1%–3%, adjusted EBIT margin (management's adjusted operating profit as a share of sales) down 60–80 basis points (0.60–0.80 percentage points), and Adjusted EPS of $1.60–$1.70. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores Inc NYSE BURL Financials_Quarterly.xls, Income Statement, FY2023–FY2025 quarterly columns; data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Outlook, 2026-08-27]

## 2. Beat Scenarios

All likelihood labels below are judgment, not measured probabilities. The available four-quarter surprise record is too short to establish an empirical frequency, and no admitted in-quarter panel read tests current demand.

| Scenario | Driver | What Would Need To Happen | Likelihood (High / Mid / Low) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue clears the high end of management's range | New-store rollout plus mature-store demand | The larger store base must continue to ramp near the Q2 pace, while comparable-store sales land near or above the +3% high end. In Q2, new and non-comparable stores supplied $254.8m of the $296.8m sales increase; the capacity contribution can carry total sales if mature-store demand does not weaken. | Mid — judgment, based on one reported Q2 bridge and current guidance | [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, MD&A — Results of Operations (Net sales), filed 2026-08-27; data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Outlook, 2026-08-27] |
| Value investment lifts Fall demand | Tariff-refund price investment, merchandise availability and reserve inventory | The planned Q3 investment of about $22m (40% × $55m) must draw customers without requiring larger markdowns, helped by the company's available reserve inventory and lapping the prior Q3 weather-related issues cited by management. Management said Q3 sales had upside potential but kept guidance because of external risks; this is not a confirmed sales benefit. | Mid — judgment; the investment is disclosed, but its sales elasticity is not | [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27; data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, MD&A — Inventory, filed 2026-08-27] |
| Profit exceeds the implied cautious setup despite planned reinvestment | Merchandise margin, supply-chain savings and SG&A leverage | Underlying merchandise margin and supply-chain/SG&A savings must offset more of the price investment than management assumed, so reported adjusted EBIT margin falls by less than the guided 60–80 bps. Q2's refund-excluded adjusted EBIT-margin gain was 100 bps, but that is a historical result rather than a Q3 sensitivity. | Mid — judgment; no matched Q3 EBITDA or EBIT consensus is available | [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27; data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Outlook, 2026-08-27] |

Management's stated underlying assumption excluding the reinvestment is only a 10–30 bps margin improvement, leaving limited disclosed room for execution slippage. | Mid — judgment, based on management's stated plan rather than a quantified sensitivity | [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27] |

## 5. In-Line Print But Bad Guidance Risk

| Risk | Evidence | Why It Matters |

| In-line current quarter but guide-down | Management retained its sales guidance despite saying it saw back-half sales upside, because it also saw external risks. Q4 is the larger seasonal quarter at 31.5% of annual sales on the last three fiscal years' average. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27; data/BURL/Burlington Stores Inc NYSE BURL Financials_Quarterly.xls, Income Statement, FY2023–FY2025 quarterly columns] | Q3 can meet its range while a weaker Q4 traffic, weather or consumer view causes a full-year cut. |
| Beat current quarter but weak margin guide | Management plans to allocate 60% of the $55m refund, about $33m, to Q4 and guides Q4 operating margin down 40–60 bps. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27] | A Q3 sales beat does not remove the larger fourth-quarter reinvestment and margin test. |
| Beat EPS due to one-offs, miss quality | The Q2 tariff refund added $0.64 to Q2 EPS; management intends the full-year earnings effect to be neutral by reinvesting it in the second half. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27] | Any Q3 upside driven by spending timing rather than recurring merchandise margin or cost efficiency would not establish a repeatable earnings run rate. |
| Beat revenue but working capital deteriorates | Q2 inventory was $1,541.3m, up 8.9% year on year, while comparable-store inventory rose 11%. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, MD&A — Inventory, filed 2026-08-27] | Higher inventory can support sales, but if it becomes mismatched to weather or demand it can raise later markdown and cash-conversion risk. It is a risk, not a current deterioration finding. |

## 6. Seasonality Read

Seasonality is mildly helpful for judging Q3 but makes Q4 more important. Q3 represented an average 23.6% of annual revenue in FY2023–FY2025, versus 31.5% in Q4; therefore, the Q3 print can test whether price investment and inventory flow are working, but it will not settle the much larger holiday-quarter result. The company also calls the Fall transition important, with weather a direct demand and markdown risk. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores Inc NYSE BURL Financials_Quarterly.xls, Income Statement, FY2023–FY2025 quarterly columns; data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, Q&A, 2026-08-27]

## 7. Historical Pattern

The vendor's last four reported quarters show normalized EPS beats in all four, with a +13.1% average and +7.3% median surprise, but revenue was two beats and two misses, with only a +0.3% average surprise. This is judgment informed by four observations, not an empirical probability: it should receive limited weight, especially because the latest Q2 results included a $0.64-per-share tariff refund that management will reinvest rather than retain. [data/BURL/BurlingtonStores,IncNYSEBURLEstimatesReport.xls, Surprise sheet, CIQ FQ3 2026–FQ2 2027; data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27]

## 8. Setup Verdict

**Setup is balanced.** The most important factor is whether mature-store demand responds to the Q3 value investment: new stores supply clear capacity, but Q2 comparable-store growth was only +2% and transactions were relatively flat. The biggest risk that could flip the setup is weather-driven weak Fall traffic, which would turn the planned price investment and higher inventory into a margin cost rather than a sales benefit. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, MD&A — Results of Operations and Inventory, filed 2026-08-27; data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-08-27]

## 9. Second-Quarter Look-Ahead

The Q4 FY2026 setup is more consequential because Q4 has averaged 31.5% of annual revenue, compared with 23.6% for Q3. It also carries about $33m of the planned tariff-refund price investment and a guided 40–60 bps operating-margin decline, versus Q3's 60–80 bps decline; a Q3 beat without a credible Q4 sales and margin outlook would therefore be incomplete. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores Inc NYSE BURL Financials_Quarterly.xls, Income Statement, FY2023–FY2025 quarterly columns; data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, 2026-08-27]

## 10. Pre-Mortem

If this setup fails, the most likely error is giving too much weight to Q2's new-store growth and refund-aided earnings while assuming that lower prices will revive mature-store traffic. The evidence does not quantify the demand response to the price investment or the weather sensitivity, so a warm Fall and weak transactions could produce a sales-plus-margin miss even while total stores keep growing. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, prepared remarks and Q&A, 2026-08-27; data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, MD&A — Results of Operations and Inventory, filed 2026-08-27]

## earnings / 06_earnings-quality.md

_Source: `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md`_

# Earnings Quality — BURL

Burlington reports under U.S. GAAP in USD. Fiscal 2025 ended January 31, 2026; FY2023 had 53 weeks. “FCF” below means CFO less cash paid for property and equipment, not Capital IQ’s different, after-interest levered-FCF measure.

## 1. EBITDA → CFO → FCF Bridge (3–5 years)

USD millions. EBITDA is the Capital IQ standard calculation, not a GAAP subtotal reported by Burlington. Working-capital change is the sum of the cash-flow-statement changes in receivables, inventory, payables and other operating assets/liabilities; a positive number adds to CFO. “Other operating items” is the derived balancing component after cash taxes, cash interest and working capital, and includes non-cash D&A, stock compensation and other operating items. It is not a separately reported cash-flow line.

| Item | FY2022 | FY2023 (53 weeks) | FY2024 | FY2025 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EBITDA — CIQ standard calculation | 650.9 | 847.4 | 1,048.1 | 1,241.5 | Improving |
| Working-capital change (CFO effect) | (9.7) | 67.6 | (126.1) | 1.2 | Volatile |
| Cash taxes paid / (refund) — CIQ source sign | (208.3) | 86.2 | 170.3 | 170.9 | Normalised after FY2022 refund/sign convention |
| Cash interest paid | 51.4 | 88.1 | 84.6 | 73.1 | Stable |
| Other operating items — derived balancing component | (201.7) | 128.1 | 196.3 | 232.7 | Improving |
| **CFO** | **596.4** | **868.7** | **863.4** | **1,231.4** | Volatile / improving |
| Maintenance capex | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not assessable |
| Growth capex | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not assessable |
| Total capex — cash paid for property and equipment | 447.4 | 492.6 | 880.4 | 1,059.8 | Rising |
| **FCF (CFO − Total Capex)** | **149.0** | **376.1** | **(17.0)** | **171.6** | Volatile |
| **CFO / EBITDA %** | **91.6%** | **102.5%** | **82.4%** | **99.2%** | Healthy but variable |

FY2022–FY2025 CFO and capex are filing-based where those fiscal periods are presented; cash-tax and cash-interest detail and the standard EBITDA calculation are from the CIQ workbooks. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46; FY2024 Form 10-K, pp.52–53; CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Cash Flow and Income Statement, annual columns]

Capex split not disclosed — total capex used. FCF may understate true recurring free cash flow because the disclosed cash-paid line includes expansion spending, but it can also overstate recurring cash if a temporary operating-cash benefit is included.

For the latest TTM to August 1, 2026, CFO was $1,415.5m and FCF on this report’s definition was $412.5m. The required facts sidecar confirms the $1,415.5m CFO reading; its $107.4m “levered FCF” is after interest and is not comparable to CFO-minus-capex FCF. [CIQ Financials→Cash Flow ‘Cash from Ops.’, LTM Aug. 1, 2026; CIQ Financials→Cash Flow ‘Levered Free Cash Flow’, LTM Aug. 1, 2026]

The TTM reported FCF includes a $55.5m tariff-refund benefit to Q2 FY2026 operating cash flow. On the disclosed assumption that the full refund was cash received in the period, normalised operating FCF is about $357.0m ($412.5m − $55.5m), versus reported $412.5m. The filing says operating cash flow benefited by $55.5m but does not separately present the refund’s cash timing, so $357.0m is a conservative normalisation, not a separately reported measure. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20 and MD&A Liquidity and Capital Resources, p.30]

## 2. Cash Conversion Assessment

CFO tracked the CIQ-standard EBITDA well: conversion was 91.6%, 102.5%, 82.4% and 99.2% in FY2022–FY2025, respectively. It was above 70% in every year and below 50% in none, so the record does not show a cash-conversion breakdown. [CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Cash Flow and Income Statement, annual columns; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46]

The FY2024 dip to 82.4% coincided with a $126.1m working-capital cash use and $880.4m of capex, rather than with a collapse in CFO. FY2025 CFO recovered to $1,231.4m, but FCF remained only $171.6m because cash capex rose to $1,059.8m. This distinguishes cash-backed earnings from the separate question of how much cash is retained after the current investment programme. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.45–46]

## 3. Working Capital Trends

Days use average opening and closing balances: `DSO = 365 × average receivables ÷ revenue`; `DIO = 365 × average inventory ÷ COGS`; `DPO = 365 × average payables ÷ COGS`; `CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO`. The balance-sheet values are from the admitted CIQ annual archive, with FY2024–FY2025 filing checks; the workbook is used so the FY2022 opening balance is on the same basis. [CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Balance Sheet and Income Statement, annual columns; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.43, 45–46]

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Direction | Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Receivable days (DSO) | 2.6 | 2.7 | 2.8 | Slightly rising | Low |
| Inventory days (DIO) | 77.7 | 74.2 | 70.8 | Falling | Low |
| Payable days (DPO) | 71.9 | 62.5 | 60.4 | Falling | Low — no supplier stretching signal |
| Cash conversion cycle (DSO + DIO − DPO) | 8.5 | 14.4 | 13.2 | Longer than FY2023, improving vs FY2024 | Low / monitor |

FY2025 ending receivables rose 18.4% while revenue rose 9.4%; inventory rose 15.0% while COGS rose 7.9%. Those point-in-time comparisons require attention, but the days-based evidence points the other way: DSO rose only 0.1 day and DIO fell 3.4 days year on year. The 10-K attributes the inventory increase to comparable-store and new-store inventory following 104 net new stores, while reserve inventory fell to 40% of inventory from 46%. This does not prove there is no inventory risk, but it does not support a channel-stuffing conclusion. [CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Balance Sheet and Income Statement, FY2024–FY2025 columns; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29]

## 4. Non-GAAP Adjustments

FY2025 reported EBITDA below is a filing-derived GAAP calculation, not the CIQ standard EBITDA used in the cash bridge. Burlington’s adjusted EBITDA was only $9.2m (0.7%) above that GAAP calculation, while adjusted net income was $15.5m (2.5%) above GAAP net income. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29]

| Adjustment | Amount | Recurring? (Y/N) | Concern Level (Low / Mid / High) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Net favourable lease costs | 7.7 | Y — $15.3m, $11.2m and $7.7m in FY2023–FY2025 | Mid | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| Impairment of long-lived assets | 9.9 | Y — $6.4m, $12.9m and $9.9m | Mid | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| Litigation matters | 4.2 | Y — $1.5m, $2.5m and $4.2m | Mid | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| Debt-amendment costs | 0.1 | Y, but small — $0.1m, $4.6m and $0.1m | Low | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| One-time layaway-liability settlement gain | (12.7) | N | Low | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |
| Security-tag amortisation write-off | 11.7 | N | Low | [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |

The recurring lease-cost, impairment and litigation exclusions should not be described as wholly one-off. Their FY2025 pre-tax total is small relative to reported income, but recurrence means adjusted metrics are a useful cross-check rather than a cleaner replacement for GAAP results. Stock-based compensation is not excluded from the adjusted-earnings reconciliation. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29]

## 6. Accrual Quality Flags

[CIQ Financials Annual workbook, Balance Sheet and Income Statement, FY2024–FY2025 columns; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] |

[FY2025 Form 10-K, Critical Accounting Estimates — Revenue Recognition] |

RF-EQ-001 (rising accruals divergent from cash earnings)

The tag is emitted because two mechanical balance-sheet growth tests are positive. It is not proof that earnings are uncollected: FY2025 CFO/EBITDA was 99.2%, DIO declined and the CFO effect of working capital was roughly neutral. The single most useful follow-up is the next seasonal inventory and gross-margin disclosure, not an unsupported conclusion about channel stuffing. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.29, 45–46]

FY2025, USD millions except EPS. “Reported EBITDA” and “reported EBIT” are filing-derived GAAP calculations; Burlington does not report them as GAAP subtotals. Adjusted net income and EPS are company non-GAAP measures tax-effected for the stated adjustment set. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29]

| Trap | Triggered? (Y/N) | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = WORSE — inverted)* |

| Stock-based compensation excluded from adjusted earnings | N | FY2025 adjusted reconciliation does not add back stock compensation; $106.7m is a cash-flow non-cash add-back, not an adjusted-earnings exclusion. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.29, 46] | 5 |
| Restructuring costs recur every year | N | No separately reported recurring restructuring line was identified; recurring impairment, lease-cost and litigation exclusions are shown in Sections 4–5. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29] | 20 |

However, retail-inventory accounting uses markdown and shortage estimates; a 1% change in retail markdowns would change FY2025 markdown cost by about $2.8m. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Critical Accounting Estimates — Inventory] | 30 |

## 9. Earnings Quality Score

**73 /100 — Mostly clean but some working-capital and adjustment noise.** The key support is cash conversion above 80% in each of the last four fiscal years and a small FY2025 reported-to-adjusted gap. The score is below the top band because reported FCF is volatile during a high-capex build, several “one-off” adjustments recur, and the latest TTM cash flow includes the $55.5m tariff-refund benefit. [FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.29, 45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20]

## 10. The Single Biggest Quality Concern

The largest current-quality risk is that Q2 FY2026 results contain a tariff refund that is real cash but not repeatable operating performance. The $55.5m reduction in cost of sales added $41.3m after tax to Q2 net income of $184.3m, about 22%, and the 10-Q says it also lifted six-month CFO. This is not evidence of an accounting error, and the earlier FY2022–FY2025 cash record remains cash-backed. It does mean the latest reported TTM FCF and gross margin should not be extrapolated without removing the refund; the filing provides no evidence that an equivalent future refund will recur. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.20, 30]

# Earnings Sensitivity — BURL

All figures are USD. Burlington reports under U.S. GAAP; “adjusted EBITDA” and “adjusted EBIT” are company-defined non-GAAP measures. The quantified operating rows below use a Q3 FY2026 13-week revenue midpoint of $2,981.5m, unless stated otherwise. They are sensitivities, not forecasts. A 1-basis-point move on that revenue base is about $0.298m. The company has not disclosed sales, weather, freight, merchandise-margin, or SG&A sensitivity coefficients; those rows use the disclosed Q2 observations as a historical range and are therefore not company guidance.

## 1. Variable Selection

The six variables come from the high/mid-magnitude revenue and margin driver tables: merchandise margin, SG&A leverage, comparable-store sales, store rollout, and the planned tariff-refund price investment. Interest rates are included because they are the only variable with a company-disclosed market-risk coefficient. The business-model dependency review also flags consumer spending, weather and tariff policy; consumer demand and weather feed the comparable-sales and markdown rows rather than being treated as independently additive variables. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, MD&A—Net Sales, Gross Margin and Inventory] [data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Q2 FY2026, Outlook] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 7A, p.40]

## 2. Sensitivity Table

For the merchandise and SG&A rows, the arithmetic is $2,981.5m × 70bps = $20.9m and $2,981.5m × 50bps = $14.9m. For comparable sales, Q2's $42.0m contribution from a 2% comparable-sales gain implies $21.0m of sales per percentage point; applying the Q2 refund-excluded adjusted-EBITDA margin of 10.7% (`($375.3m − $55.5m) / $2,997.8m`) gives $2.2m per percentage point. This static-margin calculation is an inference, not a disclosed marginal-profit rate. [data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Q2 FY2026, Non-GAAP reconciliation] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, pp.3, 20; MD&A—Net Sales]

Q2 sales per recently added/non-comparable store = $254.8m / 149 = $1.71m; the same 10.7% static margin gives the profit translation. | 125 net new stores. | +$1.8m Q3-equivalent adjusted EBITDA. | 105 net new stores. | −$1.8m Q3-equivalent adjusted EBITDA. | 0% — bound; opening dates, ramp curves and incremental-store margins are not disclosed. | Low — the sales bridge is disclosed, but the ±10-store move and margin translation are inferred. | [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, MD&A—Net Sales] [data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Q2 FY2026, Outlook]
| Interest rates | $1,730.6m of floating-rate debt, after considering swaps. | A 100bp rate move changes annual cash interest by $6.3m, assuming the January 31, 2026 debt mix and borrowing level remain constant. For a 13-week comparison, $6.3m / 4 = $1.6m pre-tax. | Rates 100bp lower. | +$1.6m Q3-equivalent pre-tax earnings/cash interest; +$0.07 annual EPS if the guided 25% adjusted tax rate and Q2 diluted shares of 63.896m are held constant. | Rates 100bp higher. | −$1.6m Q3-equivalent pre-tax earnings/cash interest; −$0.07 annual EPS on the same stated assumptions. | Interest-rate swaps are already embedded in the company coefficient; 0% further management response — bound. | High for cash-interest coefficient; Medium for the EPS translation. | [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 7A, p.40] [data/BURL/BURL_Q2_2026_Earnings_PR.pdf, Q2 FY2026, Outlook] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, p.3]

The tariff-refund row should not be added to the other rows as an independent earnings case: management's stated full-year plan offsets the recognised refund through lower prices. Likewise, the merchandise, SG&A, comparable-sales and store rows share sales, mix and cost drivers, so adding them would double count.

## 3. Sensitivity Ranking

Ranking uses a Q3-like 13-week comparison where possible. “Absolute impact” is the average of the absolute bull and bear impacts. The tariff item is one-sided relative to management's stated base, so its $11.1m figure is `($22.2m + $0m) / 2`; it is not a symmetric earnings range. Interest is stated on the disclosed annual cash-interest basis and converted to a 13-week equivalent solely for comparability.

| Rank | Variable | Absolute Impact (avg of bull + bear) | Direction of Current Trend |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | Merchandise margin / markdown execution | $20.9m Q3 adjusted EBITDA | Q2 underlying contribution was +70bps; sustainability is unproven. |
| 2 | Store and SG&A leverage | $14.9m Q3 adjusted EBITDA | Q2 adjusted SG&A improved 50bps, but new stores and infrastructure also raise D&A. |
| 3 | Planned tariff-refund price investment | $11.1m Q3 adjusted EBITDA, one-sided versus guidance | Q3/Q4 reinvestment is planned; full-year effect is stated to be neutral. |
| 4 | Comparable-store sales: traffic, basket and weather | $2.2m Q2-like 13-week adjusted EBITDA | Q2 comparable sales were +2%, from basket with traffic relatively flat. |
| 5 | Store rollout / selling capacity | $1.8m Q3-equivalent adjusted EBITDA | 115 FY2026 net new stores are guided; the Q2 sales bridge remains the main revenue contributor. |
| 6 | Interest rates | $1.6m Q3-equivalent pre-tax earnings/cash interest | The direct exposure remains after swaps, but it is smaller than operating sensitivities on this basis. |

## 4. The Single Highest-Sensitivity Variable

Merchandise margin and markdown execution is the largest supportable two-sided earnings sensitivity: a repeat or reversal of the 70bp Q2 underlying contribution changes a Q3-sales-midpoint adjusted-EBITDA read by about $20.9m before tax. It is partly company-controlled through buying, pricing and markdown decisions, but depends on the availability and mix of off-price merchandise. The adverse case needs weaker demand or less favourable goods availability to force more markdowns or remove the recent margin gain; neither the filing nor the call quantifies that probability or a recovery rate. [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, Aug 27, 2026.rtf, Q2 FY2026 prepared remarks] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 1A—Merchandise supply]

## 5. Interaction Effects

The variables are linked. Warm Fall weather or lower-income consumer pressure can reduce traffic and comparable sales, leave more inventory for markdowns, and remove SG&A leverage at the same time. Conversely, the planned Q3/Q4 price investment may support customer value and comparable sales while deliberately reducing margin. Store growth adds sales capacity and may improve fixed-cost absorption, but it also raises depreciation from stores and supply-chain infrastructure. Interest rates are separate from EBITDA but can worsen household budgets and the small direct cash-interest exposure together. These links mean the table is not additive. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, MD&A—Inventory and Gross Margin] [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, Aug 27, 2026.rtf, Q2 FY2026 prepared remarks and Q&A] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 7A, p.40]

## 6. Non-Linear Or Asymmetric Risks

The adverse demand case is likely more severe than the static comparable-sales calculation: lower traffic can create both missed sales and higher markdowns while store and infrastructure costs do not fall proportionally. Burlington states it may not be able to offset a comparable-sales decline with savings initiatives. Weather can compound this risk because cold-weather apparel demand and store traffic remain partly weather-dependent, while inventory was $1,541.3m at Q2 end and comparable-store inventory was up 11% year on year. The tariff item is also asymmetric: the $55.5m benefit was a recognised Q2 event, while management plans to give it back through customer value; the available pool does not establish a repeat refund or the current tariff terms. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, MD&A—Liquidity, Inventory and Tariff Refunds] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 1—Seasonality and Item 1A]

## 7. Earnings Volatility Score

**58 /100 — higher = worse.** Earnings have material sensitivity to merchandise margin, demand and operating leverage, and Q2 includes a non-recurring tariff refund; however, the disclosed interest-rate coefficient is modest and flexible sourcing, swaps and price/value actions provide partial but unmeasured offsets. The absence of company-disclosed demand, weather and merchandise-cost coefficients limits confidence in any more precise volatility score. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-K(Mar-19-2026).doc, FY2025, Item 1A and Item 7A, p.40] [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, p.20]

The count is not a count of independent failure modes. The tariff refund is relevant to both margin and cash quality, while weak traffic, weather, price investment and markdowns are a linked downside chain.

## 5. Red-Flag Severity Verdict

**Material concerns**

The primary reports are sufficient and historical cash conversion is sound, so this is not a critical accounting or data-quality failure. But Q2’s headline strength came largely from store capacity and a finite tariff refund, while mature traffic was flat and the company has not shown the demand response to its H2 price investment. The single most dangerous red flag is a weak transaction response to that investment during the Fall season; Q3 comparable-store sales driven by transactions rather than only basket, with merchandise margin holding near the refund-excluded guide, would reduce that concern.

## 6. What The Synthesis Agent Should Know

- 11 triggered flags: 0 Critical, 7 High, 3 Medium and 1 Low; three further items are unclear and three checks are unavailable.
- The main risk is not the known refund reinvestment itself. It is whether the roughly $22.2m Q3 price investment produces enough transaction and sales response to avoid a sales-plus-markdown-plus-leverage miss.
- The earnings verdict should be **Mixed earnings setup**, not Earnings accelerating, unless Q3 proves that mature-store demand is improving on a refund-excluded margin basis.
- No formal MODULE_RULES hard data cap applies: current filings, quarterly data, cash flow, consensus and a verbatim transcript are all present. However, consensus setup should remain at the guidance-consensus agent’s **Fair** read because Q3 normalized EPS and company Adjusted EPS are unmatched definitions.
- Do not treat CIQ LTM EBITDA as filing-reported or company-adjusted EBITDA. Preserve the definition and the $79.5m filing-calculation versus CIQ LTM difference noted by the historical-financials agent.
- The margin and quality implications of the tariff refund are one linked issue, not two independent reasons to downgrade; similarly, weather, traffic, inventory and markdown risk must not be added as independent sensitivity cases.
- Missing store-cohort returns, price elasticity and operating sensitivity coefficients mean the growth and downside cases are less measurable than Q2’s headline numbers imply.
- The setup is dirtier than an earnings-growth headline suggests, but not a fraud, cash-conversion, or source-sufficiency case.

## 7. Pre-Mortem — If The Earnings Setup Fails

The most likely failure is that Burlington’s H2 price investment does not bring back transactions during a warm Fall, leaving the larger inventory position to require markdowns while sales leverage fades. Q2 can conceal this risk because 86% of its sales increase came from new and non-comparable stores and its reported profit also included the $55.5m refund; the next result would then miss on sales and margin even though the store count continues to grow. [data/BURL/Burlington_Stores_Inc_-_Form_10-Q(Aug-27-2026).doc, Q2 FY2026, MD&A—Results of Operations and Inventory] [data/BURL/Burlington Stores, Inc., Q2 2027 Earnings Call, Aug 27, 2026.rtf, prepared remarks and Q&A]

## balance-sheet-survival — module synthesis

_Source: `balance-sheet-survival/99_balance-sheet-survival-synthesis.md`_

# Balance-Sheet-Survival Module — BURL (Synthesis)

## Abstract

BURL’s 0.84x strict net leverage—net debt divided by filing-derived EBITDA, or pre-interest/tax/depreciation/amortisation profit—rose from 0.68x at FY2025, but matched-season net debt improved year over year. [Q2 FY26 10-Q, pp.5,10,12–13; FY25 10-K, p.43] At least 11.7% matures within 24 months, covered 3.15x by cash; the calculated $1.624bn bullet is due in 2031. [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Notes 3–4] $703.7m cash plus $942.0m asset-based credit availability leave no finite run-out date on normalised cash after capital spending, but the lender-test cushion is unknown. The zero-mitigation cash stress survives a 60% EBITDA fall; its first limit is a non-contractual 4.0x marker at 77.7%. [Q2 FY26 10-Q, pp.5,20,30, Note 4; CIQ Financials, LTM 2026-08-01] Verdict: Adequate; Parent cash access and covenant terms remain unclear.

## 1. Solvency Verdict

- **Verdict:** Adequate
- **Reporting basis:** U.S. GAAP operating retailer; USD millions; balance-sheet amounts are at 1 August 2026 and flow measures are latest-12-month (LTM) to that date unless stated otherwise. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, cover and financial statements]
- **Net leverage (net debt / EBITDA):** **0.84x strict basis**, using $1,215.8m of financial net debt (`$1,711.7m` Term Loan + `$186.1m` converts + `$21.8m` finance leases − `$703.7m` cash) and $1,440.2m of latest LTM filing-derived GAAP EBITDA, a calculation from GAAP lines rather than a company-reported GAAP subtotal. **Gross leverage is 1.33x on the same EBITDA basis.** The same strict net debt is 0.89x the more conservative $1,360.7m CIQ-standard EBITDA used in the stress test. Operating-lease liabilities are excluded from strict net debt and carried separately. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12–13; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29; CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export]
- **Liquidity runway (how long cash sources cover uses):** **No finite runway on the stated normalised latest-12-month free cash flow (FCF, cash from operations minus total capital spending) run-rate**; $1,645.7m of committed liquidity equals $703.7m cash plus $942.0m disclosed asset-based lending (ABL) availability, while $357.0m normalised FCF (`$412.5m` reported LTM FCF − `$55.5m` tariff refund) exceeds the $20.1m next-12-month maturity by $336.9m. This is a run-rate result, not a forecast; peak seasonal working-capital need is undisclosed and the ABL is borrowing-base-dependent. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5, p.20, p.30, Notes 3–4]
- **Maturity wall (concentrated debt due dates; % within 24 months):** **At least 11.7%**, or $223.7m comprising $20.1m in year one and $203.6m in year two; the percentage excludes unallocated long-term finance-lease timing. The largest maturity is the calculated $1,624.0m Term Loan residual due in 2031, 84.6% of financial debt. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 3–4; FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 4 — Scheduled Maturities]
- **Tightest covenant + headroom (distance before a lender test fails):** **Not assessable.** No maintenance threshold, current covenant calculation, covenant-EBITDA definition, addback cap, springing trigger, or cure right is disclosed. The 3.50x ratio in Schedule I is a restricted-payment condition, not proven to be a live maintenance test. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 1; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- **Stress break point (EBITDA decline that breaks it):** **No contractual break point is assessable.** In the zero-mitigation bound, no modelled cash break occurs through a 60% EBITDA decline; the first displayed limit is the explicitly non-contractual 4.0x maximum-strict-net-leverage marker at a **77.7%** decline. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4; CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export]
- **Solvency strength /100:** **70**, capped because $186.1m of Parent debt is material and exact subsidiary-upstreaming access is unclear.
- **Liquidity runway /100:** **82**, reflecting the $1,645.7m liquidity build above and positive normalised FCF, reduced for undisclosed peak seasonal need and borrowing-base sensitivity.
- **Refinancing risk /100 (higher = worse; inverted):** **24**, reflecting cash coverage of the next 24 months but the concentrated 2031 residual.
- **Covenant headroom /100:** **Not assessable**
- **Downside resilience /100:** **80**, reflecting cash survival through the zero-mitigation −60% case, reduced because contractual covenant survival cannot be tested.
- **Data quality /100:** **78**, with recent filings, cash flow, maturities and ABL availability but no usable covenant test or primary rating report.
- **Overall usefulness /100:** **75**, hard-capped by the absence of a usable covenant-compliance test.
- **Biggest solvency risk:** A severe inventory and working-capital shock could reduce both the $357.0m normalised FCF run-rate (`$412.5m` reported LTM FCF − `$55.5m` tariff refund) and the $942.0m borrowing-base availability while $2,558.5m of purchase commitments and $5,735.1m of gross operating-lease commitments (`$5,124.6m` future minimum payments + `$610.5m` uncommenced leases) still require cash over their respective periods. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.20, Note 3, Note 4]

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Strict leverage omits $3,992.6m of recognised operating-lease liabilities; CIQ’s $5,202.4m lease-inclusive net-obligation measure (`$1,913.6m` debt carrying value + `$3,992.6m` operating leases − `$703.7m` cash) is 3.82x its $1,360.7m LTM EBITDA, so the 0.84x headline does not capture the full fixed-cost burden. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 3; CIQ Financials, Balance Sheet and Income Statement, Q2/LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export]
- **Strongest bull point:** $703.7m of cash alone covers the at-least $223.7m next-24-month maturity load (`$20.1m` in year one + `$203.6m` in year two) 3.15x, while EBITDA covers gross interest 18.4x. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5, Notes 3–4; CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export]
- **Single killer risk:** An inventory shock that both turns FCF negative and cuts the ABL borrowing base could remove the facility precisely when purchase and lease commitments draw cash; no borrowing-base stress sensitivity is disclosed. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 3, 4 and 11]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Evidence against the conservative Adequate call is that strict net debt is $75.9m lower than at the same seasonal point a year earlier, and the zero-mitigation −60% EBITDA cash case remains positive. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5; CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export]

Exact distribution baskets and the current 3.50x restricted-payment calculation are not disclosed. The covenant cap applies because no maintenance test or covenant-EBITDA definition is disclosed. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4 and p.30; FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 1]

## 5. Survival Summary

BURL has $1,919.5m of gross financial debt (`$1,711.7m` Term Loan + `$186.1m` converts + `$21.8m` finance leases) and $1,215.8m of strict net debt after $703.7m cash. Gross leverage is 1.33x and strict net leverage is 0.84x latest LTM filing-derived GAAP EBITDA; net leverage worsened from the fiscal year-end, but strict net debt improved by $75.9m year over year on the matched seasonal date. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12–13; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.43] The at-least $223.7m due within 24 months (`$20.1m` year one + `$203.6m` year two) is covered 3.15x by cash, so it is self-funded on the consolidated balance-sheet read; the refinancing dependence sits mainly in the calculated $1,624.0m 2031 Term Loan residual. Cash of $703.7m plus $942.0m of ABL availability and the normalised FCF run-rate support no finite runway end, but the ABL depends on its borrowing base and Parent cash access is not quantified. Contractual covenant proximity cannot be stated, despite 18.4x EBITDA/interest and 4.8x post-capex EBITDA/interest coverage. The zero-mitigation bound shows no cash-driven need for an equity raise or distressed asset sale at 30%, 40% or 60% EBITDA declines; the −60% cash result remains positive, but survival without a covenant waiver cannot be tested. [CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]

## 6. What Would Change The Solvency Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Strengthen It | What Would Weaken It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adequate | A current compliance certificate showing wide contractual headroom and unrestricted subsidiary distributions; funding the $186.1m 2027 Parent convert without materially reducing liquidity; strict net debt declining on matched seasonal dates. | Normalised FCF turning negative, a material reduction in the $942.0m ABL availability, blocked Parent access to subsidiary cash, or a refinancing plan that leaves the $1,624.0m 2031 bullet exposed as it approaches. | The current executed Term Loan/ABL credit agreement or compliance certificate, including maintenance thresholds, covenant EBITDA, addbacks and caps, springing triggers, cure rights, current ratios, and distribution baskets. |

*The strengthen/weaken tests are module judgment, not company guidance.*

## 6A. Survival Playbook (non-speculative levers)

- **Refinancing actions already taken:** BURL repaid a $50.6m promissory note in February 2026, exchanged $111.0m of converts in March 2026, extended the ABL to July 2030 in July 2025, and added $500m of Term B-7 loans in June 2025. These actions show prior execution, not a committed plan for the remaining $186.1m converts or the 2031 bullet. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- **Asset sales:** No asset-sale programme is announced in the available specialist evidence.
- **Capex cuts:** The filing gives an approximately $875m FY2026 net-capex plan, but the specialists found no evidence establishing how much can be cut without harming the store and supply-chain programme. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.30]
- **Shareholder returns:** The remaining $217.6m repurchase authorisation is discretionary and no dividend is committed. *Inference, not from filings:* suspending future buybacks would preserve cash. BURL spent $167.4m on repurchases in the first half. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 8 and p.30]
- **Covenant amendments:** No prior amendment pattern or lender commitment supporting a future waiver is evidenced in the specialist outputs.

## 7. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- Financial gross debt is $1,919.5m (`$1,711.7m` Term Loan + `$186.1m` converts + `$21.8m` finance leases); less $703.7m cash, strict net debt is $1,215.8m. Gross leverage is 1.33x and strict net leverage is 0.84x filing-derived LTM GAAP EBITDA. The rise from 0.68x FY2025 net leverage was cash-driven rather than gross-debt-driven, while strict net debt was $75.9m lower year over year at the same seasonal point. The later $1,624.0m 2031 Term Loan residual is the main refinancing concentration, with no committed refinancing plan in the pool. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 3–4; FY2025 Form 10-K, Note 4]
- Committed liquidity is $1,645.7m, built as $703.7m cash plus $942.0m disclosed ABL availability. Normalised FCF is $357.0m (`$412.5m` reported LTM FCF − `$55.5m` tariff refund), leaving $336.9m after the $20.1m next-12-month maturity; peak seasonal working-capital need is undisclosed and the ABL is borrowing-base-dependent. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5, p.20, p.30, Note 4]
- Covenant headroom is **Not assessable**. The 3.50x ratio is a restricted-payment condition, and the current contractual calculation, maintenance thresholds, covenant EBITDA, addbacks, caps, springing trigger and cure rights are not disclosed. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 1; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- The largest live debt-like exposure is $3,992.6m of recognised operating-lease liabilities against $5,124.6m of future minimum lease payments plus $610.5m for uncommenced leases. Separately, purchase commitments are $2,558.5m and outstanding letters of credit are $58.0m; these are mixed bases and are not a simultaneous-loss total. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 3 and 11]
- **RF-OBS-001 (contingent-liability spike)**
- The zero-mitigation bound has no modelled cash break through −60% EBITDA; that case remains cash-positive. The first displayed threshold is the non-contractual 4.0x strict-leverage marker at −77.7%; the real covenant break point is unknown. [CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- *Inference, not from filings:* strict net leverage of 0.84x, $703.7m cash and $942.0m of ABL availability provide counter-cyclical flexibility to keep investing when weaker rivals may have to pull back, but the $3,992.6m recognised lease liability means this is not a net-cash balance sheet. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5, Notes 3–4]

## 8. Simple Summary

- Financial debt is $1.920bn gross (`$1.712bn` Term Loan + `$186.1m` converts + `$21.8m` finance leases); less $703.7m cash, strict net debt is $1.216bn. Gross leverage is 1.33x and strict net leverage is 0.84x filing-derived LTM GAAP EBITDA. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12–13; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29]

- Committed liquidity is $1.646bn (`$703.7m` cash + `$942.0m` ABL availability). The normalised FCF run-rate produces a surplus, so there is no finite runway end on that stated basis. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 20, 30, Note 4]
- The tightest contractual covenant and its headroom are unknown. The 77.7% zero-mitigation stress marker is not a BURL covenant. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 1; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- Recognised operating-lease liabilities are $3.993bn; gross lease commitments are $5.125bn plus $610.5m uncommenced, and purchase commitments are $2.559bn. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Notes 3 and 11]

The −60% case remains cash-positive. [CIQ Financials, Income Statement, LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4]
- No primary rating-agency report or usable covenant-compliance certificate is available; the CIQ BB+ field is only a vendor screen. [CIQ Comparable Analysis, Credit Health Panel, 2026-09-28 — vendor export]

## 6. Sufficiency Verdict

- **Verdict:** Partial
- **Reason:** A recent balance sheet, cash flow statement, debt note, maturity information, and disclosed ABL availability permit the capital-structure, liquidity, coverage, contingencies, and stress work, but the pool does not provide a usable maintenance-covenant test or covenant-EBITDA definition.
- **Sections that can run:** capital structure; maturity wall; liquidity; coverage (with reported interest); contingencies; stress test. Covenant headroom can only be reported as not assessable.
- **Active partial-data caps:**
  - Covenant headroom = Not assessable; Overall usefulness max 75.
  - Covenant confidence is capped because the covenant EBITDA definition, addback caps, and current compliance calculation are absent.
- **Critical missing items:**
  - Executed ABL / term-loan credit agreement or a current covenant-compliance certificate showing the applicable test, threshold, covenant EBITDA definition, addbacks, caps, and current measurement.
  - Primary credit-rating-agency report; the CIQ rating field is only a vendor screen.
- **Single highest-value missing document:** credit agreement

_Source: `balance-sheet-survival/01_capital-structure-and-leverage.md`_

# Capital Structure & Leverage — BURL

Burlington Stores, Inc. is a U.S. GAAP operating company reporting in USD. Amounts are USD millions and are measured at August 1, 2026 unless stated otherwise. “Strict” net debt means interest-bearing financial debt, including finance leases, less cash and cash equivalents; it excludes operating-lease liabilities, consistent with §15. This report does not make a solvency verdict.

## 1. Debt Stack

| Instrument | Amount | Entity (HoldCo/OpCo) | Secured? | Seniority | Collateral | Maturity | Rate (fixed/floating) | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Short-term debt / current portion | 20.1 | BCFWC / finance-lease lessees; detailed split below | See respective instruments | See respective instruments | See respective instruments | Within 12 months | Not disclosed separately | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, filed 2026-08-27, p.5 (balance sheet); Note 3, p.10; Note 4, p.12] |
| 2027 Convertible Senior Notes (long-term) | 186.1 | Burlington Stores, Inc. (Parent) | No | Senior, unsecured | None disclosed | 2027-12-15 | 1.25% fixed; effective rate 1.7% | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4, pp.12–13] |
| Senior secured Term Loan Facility — long-term portion | 1,694.1 | BCFWC and guarantor subsidiaries / holding companies | Yes | Senior secured | First lien on equity interests, equipment, IP, certain leases/real estate and related proceeds; second lien on other assets, subject to exceptions | 2031-09-24 | Adjusted SOFR (0% floor) + 1.75%; 5.5% rate at 2026-08-01 | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4, pp.12–13] |
| ABL senior secured revolving facility (drawn) | 0.0 | BCFWC and guarantors | Yes | Senior secured | First lien on inventory, receivables, bank accounts and related proceeds; second lien on remaining assets other than real estate, subject to exceptions | 2030-07-25 | SOFR + 1.125%–1.375%; availability-based margin | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4, pp.13–14] |
| Finance / capital leases — long-term portion | 19.2 | Operating lease lessees; entity split not disclosed | Not disclosed separately | Not disclosed separately | Not disclosed separately | Payments extend beyond 2030 | 5.5% weighted-average discount rate; not a coupon | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 3, p.10] |
| **Total gross debt** | **1,919.5** | Consolidated | — | — | — | — | — | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12–13, 30] |

The $20.1m current row consists of the $17.5m current debt line plus $2.6m current finance-lease liability. The Term Loan Facility amount in the debt note is $1,711.7m including its current portion; the finance-lease obligation is $21.8m including its current portion. Thus gross debt is `$17.5m + $2.6m + $1,694.1m + $186.1m + $19.2m = $1,919.5m`. It is an obligation amount before $5.9m of unamortized deferred financing costs; the balance-sheet carrying debt after those costs is $1,913.6m. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12]

The term loan remains floating-rate, but swaps cover $1.1bn of notional at fixed rates of 2.83%–3.76%. The FY2025 filing measured a 100-basis-point rate move, after swaps, as a $6.3m annual cash-interest change at then-current debt. That is a filing sensitivity, not a forecast for the August balance. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 7A, p.40; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 5]

Future minimum payments are $5,124.6m; an additional $610.5m of committed leases had not yet commenced. | [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 3, pp.10–11] |

The CIQ annual workbook reports $17.9m of FY2025 defined-contribution-plan cost, which is an expense rather than a funding deficit. | [Capital IQ Financials Annual workbook, Pension/OPEB, FY2025 column — vendor export] |

The operating-lease liability is the reason that a lease-inclusive view is much higher than the financial-debt view. It should be carried as a separate fixed-charge exposure, not silently relabelled as strict net debt.

The strict $1.216bn figure is the canonical net-debt number for downstream agents. The required CIQ sidecar instead reports total debt of $5,906.1m, net debt of $5,202.4m and LTM EBITDA of $1,360.7m, producing 3.82x net debt/EBITDA. This is reconciled, not overridden: CIQ’s debt total includes the $3,992.6m U.S.-GAAP operating-lease liability and uses debt after deferred financing costs (`$1,913.6m + $3,992.6m = $5,906.1m`). Its $5,202.4m net figure is therefore a **lease-inclusive vendor obligation measure**, not §15 broad net debt (which would net liquid investments). [CIQ facts sidecar, Capital IQ Financials→Balance Sheet/Income Statement, Q2/LTM 2026-08-01 — vendor export; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5, 10, 12]

## 5. Leverage Ratios

Latest LTM “reported EBITDA” below is a filing-derived GAAP calculation of $1,440.2m, not a GAAP subtotal reported by BURL. It is the consistent calculation used in the earnings cross-module read. Company-defined adjusted LTM EBITDA is $1,461.1m: FY2025 adjusted EBITDA of $1,293.3m, less prior-year first-half adjusted EBITDA of $483.8m, plus current first-half adjusted EBITDA of $651.6m. The latest LTM is not a mid-cycle run rate: Q2 includes a $55.5m tariff refund in cost of sales. [FY2025 Form 10-K, p.29 (Adjusted EBITDA reconciliation); Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.3, 20, 29 (H1 reconciliation and tariff refund)]

| Ratio | On Reported EBITDA | On Adjusted EBITDA | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Gross debt / EBITDA | 1.33x | 1.31x | `$1,919.5m ÷ $1,440.2m` / `$1,919.5m ÷ $1,461.1m`; debt and EBITDA bases above. |
| Net debt / EBITDA — **strict** basis | 0.84x | 0.83x | `$1,215.8m ÷ $1,440.2m` / `$1,215.8m ÷ $1,461.1m`; strict basis. |
| Debt / capital | 48.9% | n/a | `$1,919.5m ÷ ($1,919.5m + $2,002.2m common equity)`; equity from [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5]. |
| Debt / equity | 95.9% | n/a | `$1,919.5m ÷ $2,002.2m common equity`; [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5]. |
| Net debt / normalised EBITDA — strict basis | 1.28x | n/a | `$1,215.8m ÷ $947.0m`, where $947.0m is the FY2022–FY2025 average CIQ-standard EBITDA. *Inference, not from filings; a mid-cycle proxy for this consumer- and weather-exposed retailer.* [Capital IQ Financials Annual workbook, Income Statement, FY2022–FY2025 — vendor export; FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A, pp.6–11] |

The 0.84x latest strict net-leverage ratio is not comparable with CIQ’s 3.82x, because the latter includes operating leases and uses CIQ standard EBITDA. For context only, CIQ’s lease-inclusive net obligations of $5,202.4m equal 3.61x the $1,440.2m filing-derived GAAP EBITDA, or its stated 3.82x using CIQ’s $1,360.7m EBITDA. Neither is the canonical §15 net-debt ratio.

## 6. Leverage Trend

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Latest | Direction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Net debt (strict §15 basis) | 483.3 | 716.1 | 849.8 | 1,215.8 | Up versus fiscal year-end |
| Net debt / EBITDA (same strict basis) | 0.57x | 0.68x | 0.68x | 0.84x | Up versus fiscal year-end |

The fiscal-year trend is upward: strict net debt rose $732.5m from FY2023 to the latest point, and the ratio rose from 0.57x to 0.84x. The near-term driver is cash rather than higher gross financial debt: cash fell $528.8m in H1 FY2026 while BURL spent $426.7m on reported capital expenditures, $167.4m on repurchases, and $128.6m in cash in the convertible-note exchange. [FY2024 Form 10-K, pp.50, 52–53; FY2025 Form 10-K, pp.43, 45–46; Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.5–6, 30; Note 4, p.13]

There is a relevant counter-series: at the same seasonal point one year earlier, strict net debt was $1,291.7m, so the latest $1,215.8m is $75.9m lower year on year. This does not overturn the fiscal-year-end direction; it shows that the current increase from $849.8m at January 31 is seasonal and capital-deployment-related, while the same-date comparison has improved. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5; FY2025 Form 10-K, p.43]

## 6A. HoldCo / OpCo & Structural Subordination

| Item | Evidence | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Where debt sits | The Parent issued the $186.1m convertible notes. BCFWC and guarantors hold the $1,711.7m Term Loan Facility and the $1.0bn ABL commitment; BCFWC and Burlington Merchandising Corporation have joint-and-several intercompany promissory-note obligations to the Parent for the convertibles. | Parent-note holders depend on value and cash moving up from operating subsidiaries. *Inference, not from filings:* this creates structural-subordination exposure to operating-company secured creditors. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4, pp.12–14; FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 4] |
| Upstreaming constraints | BURL says it is a holding company and its ability to pay dividends depends on subsidiary distributions. The FY2025 parent-only schedule says Term Loan Facility distributions require no default and consolidated leverage no greater than 3.50x; the current covenant calculation and distribution baskets are not disclosed in the available data. | The accounting 0.84x strict ratio is not a covenant calculation, so it cannot prove upstream headroom. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.30; FY2025 Form 10-K, Schedule I, Note 1] |
| Material restricted / trapped cash | No restricted or trapped-cash amount is separately disclosed at 2026-08-01. | Strict net debt uses all $703.7m cash; the usability of any cash subject to upstream restrictions is not separately quantified. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, p.5; p.30] |

Detailed contractual cross-default terms, rating-linked pricing steps and the full parent/subsidiary distribution baskets are not disclosed in the admitted data pool. The FY2025 10-K nevertheless says that a default or acceleration under one debt instrument could trigger default under others. The 2027 convertible notes also contain a fundamental-change repurchase right at 100% of principal plus accrued interest. [FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A (Debt risk factors); Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, Note 4, pp.12–13]

## 7. Leverage Anchor Summary (canonical numbers for downstream agents)

- **Gross debt:** **$1,919.5m**, financial debt including finance leases and excluding operating leases; this is `$1,711.7m` Term Loan Facility + `$186.1m` convertible notes + `$21.8m` finance leases, before $5.9m deferred financing costs. [Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, pp.10, 12, 30]
- **Canonical net debt:** **$1,215.8m strict §15 basis** (`$1,919.5m − $703.7m` cash). **Broad net debt is also $1,215.8m**, because no incremental liquid short-term investment balance is reported. Do not substitute the CIQ $5,202.4m lease-inclusive measure for either figure.
- **Cash and liquid investments:** **$703.7m cash and equivalents; $0.0m separately reported liquid short-term investments.** Restricted/trapped cash is not separately disclosed.
- **EBITDA base:** **$1,440.2m latest LTM filing-derived GAAP EBITDA** and **$1,461.1m latest LTM company-defined adjusted EBITDA**. Both are latest, not normalised; Q2 includes a $55.5m tariff refund. The normalised sensitivity proxy is **$947.0m** four-year CIQ-standard EBITDA, labelled inference rather than a reported EBITDA base.
- **Net debt / EBITDA:** **0.84x strict / filing-derived GAAP** and **0.83x strict / company-defined adjusted**. On the normalised CIQ-standard proxy, strict net leverage is **1.28x**.
- **Reporting currency:** **USD millions.**

The material qualification downstream agents must carry is the split between financial debt and leases: operating-lease liabilities are $3,992.6m and CIQ’s $5,202.4m vendor net-debt figure is lease-inclusive. The strict $1.216bn figure is the canonical leverage anchor; the lease liability remains a separate fixed-commitment risk.
